utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-95-13/1-A, the Prosecutor versus Mile Mrksic and Veselin Sljvancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask Messrs. Mrksic and Sljivancanin if they can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation. Mr. Mrksic. THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can follow the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sljivancanin. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Helen Brady appearing on behalf of the Prosecution. With me today are my co-counsel, Mr. Paul Rogers, Mr. Marwan Dalal, Ms. Najwa Nabti, and our case manager, Ms. Alma Imamovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. Appearances for Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all in the courtroom. For the Defence of Mr. Mrksic today, Miroslav Vasic and Vladimir Domazet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Appearances for Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin this morning, Novak Lukic, his lead counsel, is present; Maja Dokmanovic, legal assistant; Ms. Marie-Claude Fournier, legal assistant; and myself, Stephane Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Now, as you all know, this is a continuation of the appeal hearing in the case of the Prosecutor against Mile Mrksic and Veselin Sljivancanin. I would like to thank the parties for addressing some of the specific issues raised in the addendum to the scheduling order of 12 December 2008, and I would invite the parties to address those questions which were not covered on Wednesday. Today's proceedings will proceed according to the amended timetable I circulated in court on Wednesday, and we will start from a reply by the appellant, Sljivancanin's reply, 30 minutes. Counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin, would you please start.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I will have the honour of beginning this morning on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin. However, before I do so, there's a matter which was brought to my attention. On Wednesday, when we were arguing, my colleague here beside me, Ms. Marie-Claude Fournier, was in the courtroom, and we did introduce her. However, it was brought to my attention there might be some difficulty because she's not officially assigned to the case. However, Mr. President, there is a confidentiality undertaking on her behalf between everything she learns while she works with me, and I kindly ask for leave that she can be attending the proceedings, even though there might be some parts of the session which might be heard in closed session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I take it Ms. Brady has no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: No, we have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Permission granted. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours, and I thank my colleagues from the Prosecution. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all my colleagues in the courtroom. Mr. President, the first issue I would like to address this morning, on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin's further reply to the Prosecution response, relates to our third ground of appeal, and that is the notion of duty. Having read the transcript, including what my colleague mentioned on Wednesday - and that was at pages 174 and following - as well as your own observations, Mr. President, at pages 151 to 153, I wish to ensure this morning that I don't leave the Appeals Chamber with the wrong impression concerning the requirement that prisoners of war be well treated at all times. That being said, I would like to confirm and clarify our position on this issue, which is as follows: Mr. President, pursuant to Article 13 of the Geneva Convention 3, prisoners of war must be treated at all times humanely. This implies, of course, that they must be protected, particularly against acts of violence. Pursuant to Article 12 of Geneva Convention 3 as well as pursuant to the commentary to the same convention, the responsibility for the treatment and the protection of prisoners of war is a dual responsibility. This responsibility rests, of course, on the state which holds prisoners of war as well as on agents of that state. All members of the military within a state are agents of the state. Accordingly, it can be said that all members of the armed forces of a state have an obligation to treat prisoners of war humanely, and in some circumstances, Mr. President, a specific duty to protect them. For the state, the duty is triggered as soon as prisoners of war are in the custody of the state. For members of the armed forces, that duty to protect can be triggered in two ways: Firstly, if a member of the armed forces captures a prisoner of war and has a prisoner of war in his custody, then definitely he has a duty to protect that prisoner of war. Secondly, a member of the armed forces may be entrusted by his commander, who is the de jure person having the authority or the responsibility, and he can give that duty to the member of the armed forces within his unit. The best example of this, Mr. President, is that of soldiers who are assigned specifically as guards within a prisoner of war facility. Now, how can a soldier be entrusted with that responsibility or a member of the armed forces? This can happen in two ways. A member of the armed forces may have a duty to protect by virtue of the position they hold in the unit. Members of the armed forces may also have a duty to protect pursuant to the orders and the tasks issued to them by their commander. It is our position, Mr. President, that the responsibility which stems from the duty to protect that a member of the armed forces might be entrusted with is limited to one of two things; the specific attributions which goes with the post being held by that member, or the specific limitations of the orders and tasks issued to him by his commander. In this case, prisoners of war were in the custody of Operational Group South, which implies that the commander of that unit, by virtue of his position, had the de jure -- as the de jure person, having the duty to protect them. As for Mr. Sljivancanin, in his capacity as security organ of Operational Group South, it is our position that he did not have any specific duty to protect the prisoners of war. That's a proposition the Prosecution agrees with, as we have heard on Wednesday. It follows in our submissions that if Mr. Sljivancanin had a duty to protect prisoners of war on 20 November 1991, it is limited, as we heard on Wednesday, to what -- to that responsibility which was bestowed on him specifically by his commander, Mile Mrksic. Consequently, Mr. President, it is our position that at best, Mr. Sljivancanin had a duty to protect the prisoners of war at the Vukovar Hospital and while directing the triage at the Vukovar Hospital. At paragraph 391 of the judgement, contrary to our third ground of appeal, the first sub-ground, the Trial Chamber found the following: The Trial Chamber said Mr. Sljivancanin's responsibility extended to ensuring that the war crimes suspects were transported to the prison at Sremska Mitrovica, whereas the civilians were to go to Sid in Serbia or to the Croatian border. In either case, pursuant to the finding of the Trial Chamber, Mr. Sljivancanin was to transport them to their destination. Our position, Mr. President, is that if the Appeals Chamber confirms this finding, contrary to our ground of appeal, once the prisoners of war were at the JNA barracks and the plan was changed whereas instead of going to Sremska Mitrovica, Mile Mrksic decided to send them to Ovcara, at that time Mr. Sljivancanin no longer had any duty or any specific duty to protect the prisoners of war. From that moment on, Mr. President, Mr. Sljivancanin was kept out of the loop, and it is his commander who was responsible, as the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 300, who was responsible for the transport of the prisoners of war, their security, and their ultimate decision as to where they would go -- destination, sorry. The commander of Operational Group South was issuing orders to other officers and receiving information in relation to what was happening to the prisoners of war through other officers. From that moment on, there was no more specific responsibility bestowed on Mr. Sljivancanin. I would now like to address the Prosecution's submissions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, does this really make sense, in terms of simple common sense, a unit or an officer is entrusted with responsibility for POWs? The first destination is a, and then the destination is changed to B. This officer can say, Goodbye, goodbye, I have finished my responsibilities, I can leave those people without caring for their minimum needs or when there are paramilitaries around particularly, who are screaming for blood. In time of war, surely there is some kind of flexibility in terms of destinations of transfer. Those things change constantly, according to tactical situations. So can you just say, My job is done, I can now start reading "The New York Times" and relax? You know, counsel, we need common sense in interpreting international humanitarian law, and there are certain objects which are deeply rooted in the Geneva Conventions, and the idea is that there is a very fundamental duty of care and that basically you have to perform those duties until you hand those duties over to somebody who could take care of the welfare of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you for your observation, Mr. President, and I'm glad that you mention both two things; first of all, the flexibility of wartime conditions and tactical conditions, as well as the fact that once a duty has been removed from a person, that person no longer has that duty. Now, in the facts of this case, this is what happened: Mr. Sljivancanin had some kind of tasking and responsibility in respect of the triage in the Vukovar Hospital, and from that point on the buses left, and he knows where the buses were going, and the facts establish that his deputy is sitting on that bus. So at that point on, there's no problem. However, once that duty is removed from him because that duty is given to somebody else for a different reason, this is what the facts of this case establish, that from the moment that there was a decision, those people would not be going to Sremska Mitrovica, but they would be handed over to members of the TO and paramilitaries over at Ovcara. From that point on, Mr. President, when that decision was made, the responsibility was removed from Mr. Sljivancanin. It's not that he ignored the responsibility. He was at the hospital, as the facts relieve. He was handling the care of all the civilians who were there. He was acting according to the responsibilities which he was entrusted with by taking care of those civilians, and he did that until 2.30 in the afternoon. At that point on, he had lost that responsibility. It was given to somebody else. Thank you, Mr. President. I would now like to address the Prosecution's submissions in relation to Ground 2 of our appeal, and Ground 2 raises the question, of course, whether aiding and abetting by omission, in the specific form recognised by the Trial Chamber, is recognised under the Statute of this Tribunal. The Prosecution at page 163 does exactly what we respectfully submit the Trial Chamber did. It confuses omission liability as a principal perpetrator for a culpable omission and aiding and abetting by providing moral encouragement or moral support to the perpetrators of a crime; that is, by being present at the scene of a crime. That is exactly what we ask the Appeals Chamber, Mr. President, to address. In our submission, omission as a principal perpetrator requires three things; that the accused had a duty to act, pursuant to criminal law; that he deliberately failed to act -- fulfill his duty; and that he intended the consequences or was aware of the consequences arising from his failure to act, and he accepted them. In this case, even if the Appeals Chamber was to confirm that Mr. Sljivancanin had a duty to protect the prisoners of war at Ovcara, there is no evidence that he intended the consequences or that he was aware of the consequences and that he accepted them. Consequently, the Trial Chamber could not, in our view, Mr. President, find him guilty for an omission as a principal perpetrator, and it is also our respectful submission that the Appeals Chamber could not, on the basis of the evidence, of course, change the Trial Chamber's verdict from aiding and abetting by omission to a culpable omission. On the other hand, Mr. President, there is commission by omission, where the accused provides encouragement and moral support, and this requires the following, that the accused be present or very close to the scene of a crime; that the presence of the accused at the scene or very close; provides encouragement or moral support to the perpetrators in the sense that it contributes substantially to the commission of the crime by them; and, finally, that the accused knew that by being present at the scene or close to the scene of a crime, that he was assisting the perpetrators in the commission of a crime. It must be noted regarding commission by omission pursuant to moral encouragement that it is not necessary, in our view, that the accused have a positive duty to act, although as I explained Wednesday, this may become relevant. In this case, the Trial Chamber rightly found that Mr. Sljivancanin did not provide any encouragement or moral support to the perpetrators of the mistreatment of prisoners of war at Ovcara. Consequently, the Trial Chamber could not find him guilty for commission by omission, and it is our respectful submission that the Appeals Chamber could not, again, on the basis of the evidence on the record, change the Trial Chamber's verdict from aiding and abetting by omission to that of commission by omission. In support of these submissions, we respectfully refer the Appeals Chamber to pages 162 and 163, where my colleague from the Prosecution referred to the Blaskic case as being a situation which was similar in every respect to the facts of the present case. This is certainly not the case, Mr. President. Firstly, the Trial Chamber in this case made it clear that the facts had to be distinguished from that of Blaskic. That's the judgement at paragraph 667, referring also to paragraphs 553 and 554. Secondly and more importantly, when Blaskic omitted to take action in respect of civilians who were used as human shield, the persons committing the offence were his direct subordinates. The civilians detained in front of his headquarters were in his immediate custody. His failure to do anything relates only to himself as well as to his direct subordinates. All he had to do was to issue one order to his subordinates or to cancel his own order and send the civilians back to their village. There was no action to be taken in respect of a third party trying to hurt those civilians. This is why, in these circumstances, his failure to take action was considered by the Appeals Chamber, in our respectful submission, as a deliberate and intentional omission because when he left his headquarters on that day, he must have seen the civilians held by his subordinates in front of his headquarters. He knew already that the offense of human shields, of using civilians as human shields, was being committed or, if not, already consumed, and all he had to do to protect those civilians was to cancel his own order, which was within his prerogative. He left without doing so. To the extent that Blaskic may have been convicted for aiding and abetting, which in the view taken by the Trial Chamber in this case, based on the indictment, of course, that's not clear, then it can only be that he provided moral encouragement and support to his own subordinates guarding the civilians because his subordinates knew he was there, and he condoned their actions. Both scenarios, Mr. President, are unrelated to the situation of Mr. Sljivancanin. Lastly, with respect to aiding and abetting, my colleague from the Prosecution referred to the Essen lynching case as being a case which was strikingly similar to the present case. That was at page 165. It is our submission, Mr. President, that the Essen lynching case deals with culpable omission and/or a case of inciting, both of which do not find application here. The next issue I'd like to address --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will stop here, Mr. President. I'm short of time. My colleague will take over for the remainder of the reply this morning. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Good morning to Your Honours. Good morning to all participants in the proceedings. In response to the first ground of appeal concerning the error of the Trial Chamber when they established the presence of Sljivancanin at Ovcara, the OTP did not present any arguments challenging the very essence of the Sljivancanin appeal, and those are the errors made by the Trial Chamber. Instead of that, the OTP, for the most part, repeats the arguments of the Court from the judgement without referring to the allegations from the appeal at all. The OTP, further on, gives their own assessment and interpretation of the evidence, and that is most obvious when they compare the testimony of Dodaj and P-009. Claiming that they were at different places and that they had a different perception of events is something that the Prosecutor could not and should not do, saying that that is the only thing that the Court could establish. The testimony of Witness P-009 is untenable because the Court did not establish a comparison between the testimony of these two witnesses, and that is the error that concerns the convincing quality of this testimony. We are aware of the fact that it is not the duty of the Trial Chamber to deal with each and every piece of evidence, but it is exactly the standard from the appeal judgement in Kvocka, paragraph 23, that we invoked in paragraph 76, confirms our position that that is the obligation of the Court when the evidence is clearly relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speaker please slow down. Could he please read slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What evidence can be more relevant than this kind of testimony, a witness who is there at the same time, as we see that the Prosecutor accepts, and on the other hand he doesn't see Sljivancanin. Speaking of the conclusion for the appeal decision in Nata-Kira-Timana shows the importance of this assessment that was established by the Court in that case but not here. If we look at the transcript from Wednesday, page 190, the Prosecutor claims that the Trial Chamber bore in mind these different vantage points, and that cannot be found in the judgement, so how could the OTP come to that conclusion? The two sketches that were shown to you, namely, Exhibits 238 and 282, only confirm the thesis of the Defence on the inaccuracy of the testimony of P-009. He had to pass by Dodaj and three other deserters and two high-ranking officers of the JNA, whereas he testified that he had not seen them. He states unequivocally that there and then, there weren't any officers or a group of prisoners, including Dodaj. That is what he decidedly said; transcript reference 6283. The Prosecutor refers to the testimony of Berghofer and many others about the appearance of Mr. Sljivancanin. Could this kind of face that cannot be forgotten, as Berghofer said, be imperceptible in an area that you saw on these sketches from the vantage point where Dodaj stood for over one hour? In addition to the beatings that he observed, he also testified that the colonels that he stood with showed him the fields in front of the hangar - page reference 5537 - the ignition of the bulldozer - on the same page - the arrival of officers in a jeep; 5539. He also said that he saw the departure of the buses; page reference 5540. He confirmed that he did not see any kind of digging of a hole in front of the hangar or on the other side of the road; that is to say that he observed a great deal of things, and he testified about that inter alia in response to Prosecution questions. The Prosecutor claims that the testimony of P-009 is consistent with the sequence of events on that day, which should confirm the credibility of his testimony. To be quite clear, we do not claim at all that P-009 was not in these places that are mentioned. We claim that he could not see Sljivancanin there because Sljivancanin at that time could not have been at those places. The fact that one witness, an eye-witness, testifies in that way in order to -- and we see that this fits into the sequence of events that are established by the Court, can certainly not be an argument that supports his credibility. Look at the testimony of P-022, who is also in different places, that the Court established, including the executions, but he was not credible enough in order to establish the responsibility of Captain Radic. P-009 was present and active at these places when the crimes were committed. We are not saying that he was a participant in the commission of crimes, but he claims that he did not see the crimes of beatings in the hangar; transcript reference 6284. He had an interest in terms of not telling the truth; Dodaj, no. In relation to all other errors of the Trial Chamber that the Defence indicated in the first ground of appeal, the OTP in their oral response only repeated the findings of the Court. The OTP did not give any specific answer to the paragraphs of the appeal. Instead of that, they decided to quote the paragraphs of the judgement that are being challenged. You can see that on transcript page 186-187. Thank you, Your Honours. We have completed this part of our submissions. I would kindly ask if Mr. Bourgon could deal with another subject just for another five minutes, with the permission of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: For five minutes, certainly, but please do not exceed the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I will not -- I just wish at this time to briefly address Ground 5, which the Prosecution commented upon in its response. Mr. President, it was our submission, as a ground of appeal, that it is reasonable to infer, on the basis of the totality of the evidence on the record, that if Mr. Sljivancanin was at Ovcara on 20 November 1991 and left without taking action, he did so and that he had no -- he did not know that by doing so he was assisting the commission of a crime. I mention the first reason for this, and that was the actions taken already in Ovcara which he must have seen, actions taken by both the Chief of Staff of Operational Group South and the commander of 80 Motorised Brigade, who was -- who were present. But it is our submission that the Trial Chamber should also have considered that Sljivancanin's knowledge on that day and at that time, and his knowledge, what he knew, is that as long as the prisoners of war were under the security and authority of the JNA, any attempts by members of the TO to commit crimes could be stopped and the situation placed under control. It happened that same morning at the JNA barracks, even though it is our submission that Sljivancanin was not there. Another example took place two days earlier. Under the security of the JNA, a group of prisoners of war was accommodated at Ovcara before being transferred to Sremska Mitrovica, without any incident. Moreover, the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 672 something that is very relevant. The Trial Chamber concluded that since the prisoners of war remained under the security and authority of the JNA at Ovcara, Sljivancanin could reasonably have believed in the circumstances that the TOs and paramilitaries would be unlikely to resort to killings. If he did not see, as we say, the beatings, he could also reasonably believe that the situation was under control. Thank you very much, Mr. President. This concludes our submissions in reply to the Prosecution response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Do any of my distinguished colleagues have questions? No. So we will now turn to the Prosecution. You have one hour, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So you will be addressing the Court now, Ms. Brady?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I'm addressing the Court now, Your Honours. I'd like to give, firstly, a brief outline of how we will be addressing this morning the Prosecution's appeal. As you know, we have four grounds of appeal; Ground 1, which relates to the application of Article 5, crimes against humanity to this case; Ground 2, relating to Mr. Sljivancanin's acquittal for murder; and Grounds 3 and 4, which relate to the manifest inadequacy, in our submission, of the sentences of 5 years and 20 years, respectively, given to Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Mrksic. Now, in light of the time, because we have one hour and we want to use our time efficiently and appropriately, we won't this morning be making submissions on sentence on Grounds 3 and 4, on Mr. Sljivancanin or Mr. Mrksic's sentence. We rest entirely on our briefs for those two appeals. What we will be making submissions on this morning are Ground 2, relating to the acquittal for murder, and Article 5. I anticipate that the majority of this morning's first hour will relate to that acquittal for murder - and this is Ground 2 - and I'll be making submissions on behalf of the Prosecution. At the same time, Your Honours, I will be answering both questions that Your Honours have posed in the addendum relating to this ground of appeal; firstly, the question about whether his duty continued and, secondly, whether he knew of or learned of Mrksic's order to withdraw the JNA troops. After that, Mr. Dalal, my co-counsel, will briefly answer Your Honour's question concerning Article 5, and in particular its application to the facts of this case. So if I could begin, then, on my submissions on Ground 2 relating to his acquittal for -- Mr. Sljivancanin's acquittal for aiding and abetting murder. Veselin Sljivancanin was convicted for aiding and abetting the torture of some 200 prisoners of war held at Ovcara on the 20th of November, 1991, and on the first day of this hearing, we demonstrated why this conviction, his conviction for these crimes, must be upheld. But in our submission, his criminal responsibility should not have ended there. Sljivancanin should have been convicted not only for the torture endured by the prisoners that fateful afternoon, but also for their murders later that night, the murder of 194 people, 194 people whom he was duty-bound to protect, and despite his ample powers and authority, he took no steps to prevent their impending fate, and that is what our appeal is about. In our submission, the only reasonable conclusions are the following: Firstly, that Sljivancanin knew from the time he was at Ovcara that without taking further action to protect the prisoners, the violence that he saw being unleashed upon the prisoners by the Serb TOs and paramilitaries was very likely to escalate to murder. Second, once he returned to the command post at Negoslavci that evening, his knowledge of murder escalated upon learning that the last vestiges of this security, the remaining JNA, were to be withdrawn, and I will be spending time on this in my submissions, and I'll develop this further today, especially when I answer Your Honour's third question. The third only reasonable conclusion: Sljivancanin was under a duty that day to protect the prisoners, a duty that remained on him throughout the course of the day and the night, and here, of course, I'm talking about the period after 9.00 when they were murdered, and in this regard I will be developing today in some detail this argument when I answer Your Honour's second question. Finally, by failing to take any steps to protect the prisoners from harm that afternoon and evening, Sljivancanin substantially contributed not only to their beatings and tortures, but also to their murders later that night. The Trial Chamber's reasons for acquitting Sljivancanin for the murders were, in our submission, unreasonable. Very briefly, firstly, it failed to find that he knew at the time of his visit to Ovcara that killings would be committed because in their reasoning, then the prisoners were then under JNA guard. This is its finding in relation to mens rea at paragraph 673, and in this respect, it factually erred. And having factually erred in this regard, the Trial Chamber then disregarded the entirety of his culpable omissions in the afternoon, afternoon to early evening period, that is, before the JNA withdrew, as being a substantial contribution to their later murders. The second way the Trial Chamber erred is that since the murders occurred after the JNA soldiers withdrew from Ovcara, an event which they found terminated Sljivancanin's delegated authority from Mrksic, the Trial Chamber said it could not be -- it could not be said that he failed to discharge any legal duty to the prisoners. This is their error in relation to the actus reus of the offence at paragraph 673, and in this it legally erred. Finally, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber simply failed to make any findings regarding his state of knowledge from 8.00, 8.00 p.m., when he returned to Negoslavci. Now, the relevant place it would have done this would have been -- we would have seen it in the judgement in paragraph 389, but there's no finding about whether he knew that they had been ordered to withdraw the JNA -- excuse me, there's no finding that he knew that the JNA had been ordered to withdraw, and this becomes relevant to the Trial Chamber's error in relation to duty because we're asking this Appeals Chamber to find that the Trial Chamber legally erred in finding that the duty had expired. Then, having found that the duty continued, having found the Trial Chamber committed legal error, they should have found the duty continued, you should apply this correct legal standard to the evidence in the trial record and find that he did know, at least from that point onwards at 8.00 p.m., that the prisoners would be murdered. And, indeed, as I'll show you today, it's the only reasonable conclusion. I'll turn first to the Trial Chamber's error regarding the mens rea. We call this in our brief "the knowledge error." Picture the scene that Sljivancanin must have witnessed, that the Trial Chamber found Sljivancanin must have witnessed at Ovcara that afternoon. Prisoners, many of whom were already sick or wounded, were being unloaded from the buses in groups, and then after being questioned and stripped of their valuables and identification, they were then forced to pass between two rows of TOs and paramilitaries with some 10 to 15 people on each side, all the while being beaten by the TOs and the paramilitaries using sticks, rifles, poles, chains, and other such implements. As an isolated event, this vicious scene would have been very alarming for even a casual observer, but the point is this was not an isolated event, and Sljivancanin was not a casual bystander. And I think first it's important to look at who Sljivancanin was. At the time, he was a major in what could be regarded as the most elite unit of the JNA, itself a highly-efficient and disciplined army. Mrksic had put him in charge that day of evacuating and transferring the prisoners from the hospital, including securing their safety and security, and he'd been authorised to use as many military police he needed to accomplish this mission. And now consider, if you will, Your Honours, what he already knew when he was witnessing this violent scene unfold in front of him at Ovcara. As the Trial Chamber found, he already knew of the violent behaviour and propensity of the TOs, but the Trial Chamber also found that he could have reasonably believed that they weren't in danger of being killed because at that stage they were under JNA guard, and it's this finding in paragraph 672 that was wholly unreasonable when you consider this: He knew in the preceding months that Serb TOs and paramilitaries had been increasingly antagonistic towards persons they perceived as Croat defenders. He said he'd read some of these reports of sadistic abuse and killings. He knew that only the night before at Velepromet, and despite, despite some regular JNA soldiers, that is, in the form of the Guards Motorised Brigade, military police guarding prisoners, Serb TOs and paramilitaries had not only been mistreated but killed Croat victims held there. What else did he know at that point in time while he's watching this scene unfold? He knew that that very day, in fact, just a few hours earlier, regular JNA soldiers had been present at the JNA barracks, these military in the form of the military police of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and yet still the TOs and the paramilitaries had been able to harass and violently beat prisoners from this group that were being held at the barracks en route to Ovcara. Most significantly, as Sljivancanin himself saw, again, the TOs and the paramilitaries have turned up at Ovcara, and despite the regular -- the presence of regular JNA soldiers, the TOs and the paramilitaries were able to savagely beat the prisoners as they were being unloaded, and, indeed, I note paragraph 235 of the judgement, which notes that the evidence is that some may even have joined in. I also note, in that paragraph, that there are findings that the JNA military police, who had provided security on the bus, stayed on the bus while this savage beating was going on, and the 15 to 20 JNA soldiers who were there apparently to secure the area, the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade, failed to stop the violence. Now, we acknowledge that at times, as my learned colleague has pointed out, at times the regular JNA had been able to maintain and restore some degree of order and security; for example, eventually at Velepromet when they loaded -- the night before when they loaded the prisoners onto the buses. Likewise, eventually at Ovcara -- at the JNA barracks, even for short periods at Ovcara. But at best, the security situation can be described and would have appeared to Sljivancanin as highly fragile, highly volatile, despite some briefs -- some brief lulls in the violence. The totality of the evidence demonstrates that on the whole, JNA military police and other regular JNA units had been largely ineffective in the face of Serb TO and paramilitary determination to seek revenge and harm Croat prisoners, and this was something he well knew. So by the time he was at Ovcara, Sljivancanin knew not only that Serb TOs and paramilitaries were capable of killing - that's the Trial Chamber finding at paragraph 672 - most critically and contrary - this is where we disagree with the Trial Chamber's findings - he knew that the mere presence of a relatively small group of JNA soldiers without proper instruction or leadership offered but a veneer, a veneer of protection for the prisoners, and that if left unchecked, if no action was taken to get the situation firmly under control, not only would beatings and tortures continue, but there was a real likelihood that the violence would escalate just as it had done at Velepromet the night before and that the TOs and the paramilitaries would succeed in fully satisfying their revenge and kill the prisoners, whether or not some JNA soldiers were present. Now, so far, Your Honours, I've been speaking about Sljivancanin's state of knowledge in the afternoon, and that's been important to develop because it sets the scene for what I'm about to say on his knowledge later that evening. Now, what about his knowledge when he returned to Negoslavci in the evening? And this brings me now to answer Your Honour's third question that you've asked: When did he learn about Mrksic's order to withdraw the JNA from Ovcara? The only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the totality of the evidence is that when Veselin Sljivancanin returned to the command post at Negoslavci that evening, he must have learned of Mrksic's order to withdraw the remaining JNA from Ovcara. It is simply inconceivable, based on his assigned role, based on JNA military doctrine, and based on his specific discussions that he had with the prisoners -- sorry, excuse me, specific discussions that he had about the prisoners with his two subordinates, Vukasinovic and Vukosavljevic and his commander Mrksic, upon his return, it is inconceivable that he was not so informed. Let me take you through that evidence, and I want to start, if I may, with Sljivancanin's own testimony about the conversations -- the discussions he had upon his return to Negoslavci, and I start first with Vukasinovic, his discussion with Vukasinovic, and what he says transpired, and he gives this evidence at transcript page 13663. And according to Sljivancanin, Vukasinovic told him that the prisoners had been taken to Ovcara that day and that he, Vukasinovic, had observed violent behaviour by the TOs and the paramilitaries to the prisoners, but he'd managed to regain order and that the prisoners went into a hangar secured by the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and Sljivancanin said that at this point, he was surprised to learn that they'd been taken to Ovcara. Now, of course, we know this is something the Trial Chamber did not believe him on, this surprise that the route had changed, because they found he was at Ovcara in the afternoon and that, in fact, he had been involved in that transmittal of that order for them to go to Ovcara. Now, the second conversation he has when he gets back to Negoslavci is with his subordinate Borisavljevic, and according to Sljivancanin, Borisavljevic told him that there had been a meeting of the so-called SAO government, and at this meeting, and I quote from Sljivancanin's testimony at transcript page 13664, at this meeting: "The decision had been taken for the prisoners who had been taken from the hospital to be handed over to the government so that they could be exchanged for captured Serbs." So having had these two conversations, what next does Sljivancanin do? Well, he says he went to report to Mrksic, and he was asked, Why did he go at this point to report to Mrksic, and he gives his answer at transcript page 13986. These are his reasons: "You asked me why I went to see Mrksic, and that's precisely what I am trying to explain, because of what he" - Vukasinovic - "told me, when he told me about those people going to Ovcara and not Mitnica, and also because of what Vujic had told Borisavljevic, that someone from higher up had given orders for those people to be taken over or surrendered to the government, so I went to see the commander to see whether that was in fact true." Now, just to take it in chronological order, what did Sljivancanin say Mrksic told him? Now, we have to recall, by this stage, as the Trial Chamber found, Mrksic had already -- on the Trial Chamber's finding, Mrksic had already given his order for the remaining JNA, in the form of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade, to leave Ovcara, and on the Trial Chamber's findings, he had conveyed that order through Sljivancanin's own deputy, Karanfilov. So with that in mind, what does Sljivancanin say that Mrksic told him? And again, I'm quoting from Sljivancanin's testimony, transcript page 13665. This is what he says that Mrksic told him: "We have completed our missions. The Guards Brigade is pulling out to get some rest. All the commitments in this area will be taken over by the 80th Motorised Brigade and the Vukovar TO --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters: "Today, a government meeting was held at Velepromet. They will now start setting up civilian authorities. They also took charge of a group of suspects from the hospital who had been brought to the barracks in order to later be exchanged for captured Serbs." Now, having had all this information come to him, what did Sljivancanin think? Well, when asked in cross-examination, he said -- he concluded that -- he concluded that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So having heard all this information, what did Sljivancanin think? Well, he concluded that the, quote, "security would now be taken over by a fresh, well-rested unit. They were in charge of the area, and there could be no further riots or anything there." So what did Sljivancanin do at this point? He didn't pursue the matter about the prisoners any more with his commander, Mrksic. He didn't ask any follow-up questions about their fate or their destination. Instead, he went to call General Vasiljevic, his boss in the SSNO, about an unrelated matter concerning some documents, and then, after that, he went and watched some television that evening because he heard there was going to be some footage about Vukovar that day on the TV and that there might be some footage of him on it. So, Your Honours, imagine this: He'd specifically gone to see Mrksic to voice concern about the prisoners having been taken to Ovcara and to brief him on reports of violence and to see if it was true that they were going to be handed over to this so-called government, a government that he -- a government that he had difficulties seeing was a legitimate government. Mrksic then confirms, indeed, that this hand-over to the government was -- had taken place or was going to take place. In Sljivancanin's mind, this could only have meant that the situation for the prisoners was getting even more precarious. He asked no follow-up questions about the prisoners, and he instead, in his own words, concludes that, quote "people were safe." That's at transcript 13982. Apparently, he says on the basis of being told, that the 80th Motorised Brigade was there in the area. Sljivancanin's testimony that he believed that the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade was looking after this situation is clearly a lie, just like his testimony that he did not go to Ovcara that day. This is a further example of lies that he has told in this case to distance himself and to down-play his knowledge of the events that day. It is simply inconceivable that Mrksic, in the course of a specific conversation with Sljivancanin about the prisoners, in which he confirmed that the prisoners now had custody -- were now in the custody of the government, would not only omit telling Sljivancanin this highly relevant piece of information, that he had ordered the JNA to withdraw, but would actively mislead Sljivancanin into thinking that the JNA, the 80th, would remain in Ovcara when he, in fact, had already ordered their removal. And when Mrksic himself already by this stage, on the Trial Chamber's findings, had already sternly questioned Vojnovic when he came to him that evening on why his units of the 80th were still there, it is equally inconceivable that Sljivancanin, who had been specifically entrusted by Mrksic with the transfer and security of this group of prisoners - and that's a Trial Chamber finding - and even though he knew that the TOs were beating and torturing the prisoners that day - another Trial Chamber finding - and even though he was aware of an order from the 1st MD, military district, on the 19th of November, 1991, forbidding the exchange of prisoners - that's Exhibit 442 - he did no follow-up with Mrksic about the prisoners, even though it was an inherent part of his duty that day. Sljivancanin's account simply defies military doctrine. He was in command of the evacuation. As such, he should have known at all times what his units were doing while they were carrying out the evacuation, including the military police, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, supposing that we separate for a moment the question of Sljivancanin's reason to believe that prisoners would be killed prior to his learning of the order to withdraw, now you argue regarding -- you argued and answered our question regarding when did Sljivancanin learn of Mrksic's order to withdraw. Would you clarify for us, what does from this conclusion regarding -- what would be the conclusion from that argument you made regarding the time when Sljivancanin learned of the order to withdraw concerning the mens rea component of aiding and abetting, so a view related to mens rea, possibly mens rea of Sljivancanin. And, secondly, I'm still looking forward to you specific argument regarding Sljivancanin's ongoing legal duties despite, despite the order of Mrksic to withdraw the JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I will deal with both. I'll turn to directly answering your question about how this then fulfills, assuming he knows, on the basis that he knows that the order, how it fulfils the mens rea, and rest assured, Your Honours, I will be coming in some detail to the question of the continuation of his duty in just a moment. I have to do it in order, and we chose to do knowledge first and then duty, so that's our plan this morning. Our submission is quite simple. Once he learnt that the JNA had been ordered to withdraw, he must have then known that the prisoners' murders were all but a certainty, and this is because he then knew that their last hope, the last vestige of their protection - insufficient as we say it was, but it was something - that last vestige of protection was to be removed, leaving the prisoners completely exposed to the unrestrained violence of their revenge-seeking Serb enemies, and that's how the mens rea is fulfilled upon him learning of this order, and we say in the afternoon, he knew of the likelihood of murder. By the evening, when he learns of the order to withdraw, the knowledge must be at the level of certainty by that stage. Those, Your Honours, are our submissions on why the Trial Chamber's findings about his mens rea were unreasonable and should be overturned. I'd like to now get to the second part of the equation, as it is, on why the Trial Chamber acquitted him, and that is that they found that his duty to protect the prisoners had expired by the time they were killed, and so he could not be criminally liable for failing to prevent their deaths. Now, we've highlighted -- we've developed this argument quite in full in our briefs, and in our submission, there are two aspects of this actus reus finding that are incorrect, that the Trial Chamber erred on. Firstly, this finding completely disregards Sljivancanin's earlier inactions, what he did not do earlier in the day that afternoon and evening, and here I'm talking about the time before the JNA withdrew. It simply failed to consider those as substantially contributing to the murders, and we've labelled that in our brief, for clarity's sake - I hope it is clear - the contribution error. The second error which Your Honour Judge Meron had expressed concern about in these proceedings is concerning the duty that he had, and in our submission, even if his special delegated authority for Mrksic terminated upon the JNA withdrawal, which the Trial Chamber -- happens about 9.00 p.m., his duty to the prisoners did not expire. This duty continued even after the JNA withdrew, and upon learning of the withdrawal order, meaning the prisoners were now in the sole custody of the TOs, he still did not -- he still did nothing to protect them, and this failure to discharge his legal duty substantially contributed to their murders. Now, again, if I may take this -- I think it's easier for the flow of things if I take this somewhat chronologically. I'd like to take the second issue about the duty in a moment, when I will also answer Your Honour Judge Meron's -- Your Honour's question number 2 which you've posed to the parties. I would like to say before I do that a few brief words, however, on the contribution error, as we have called it, because it's apparent when you look at paragraph 673 that the Trial Chamber only examined whether he did, in fact, breach his legal duty and thereby contributed to the murders at the point in time -- at that moment onwards from when the murders occurred, and in our submission, this approach was both artificial and wrong because his contribution to the murders began - and I'm talking about his culpable omissions - his contributions began from that time he was at Ovcara and continued up until and then throughout the time that they were killed after 9. The Trial Chamber disregards that it was his failure to act to discharge his legal duty to the prisoners throughout the afternoon and early evening, the omissions before the JNA withdrew, that did contribute substantially to the later murders. And this is why his complete inaction from about 3.00 p.m., 2.30 or 3.00 p.m., on the Trial Chamber's findings, when he was there, for the next five or six hours, not only meant that beatings and tortures continued unabated; most importantly, it meant that an environment of criminality and impunity developed and escalated at Ovcara, in effect setting the stage for the TOs and the paramilitaries to take their brutality to its ultimate conclusion. And Your Honours will recall that throughout that afternoon, he had full powers and authority for Mrksic, and he could have done a number of things to prevent the situation from getting out of control. I won't repeat them. They're in our brief. I won't repeat them in detail, but just to state: Look at all the things he could have done. He could have taken the prisoners to a place of safety. He could have given proper direction to the military police present. He could have greatly increased the numbers of military police. He could have removed once and for all the Serb TOs and paramilitaries. But not once did he take any of those basic steps. This inaction meant that over the course of the afternoon, Ovcara turned into a prelude to a killing field. Now, we are aware the Trial Chamber found no evidence that the perpetrators perceived Sljivancanin's presence as some kind of tacit approval or encouragement, but our point is different; his abject failure to meet his duties to the prisoners that afternoon, in the afternoon, meant that Ovcara became an environment increasingly conducive to unchecked violence. Let's not forget that it was during the afternoon that the beatings and the tortures continued, that the hole for the mass grave was dug, that the numbers of TO went from 30 to 300. It was just a matter of time before that violence spiraled so out of control that killings became the reality, and that's exactly what happened. So that's the first error on the actus reus finding in paragraph 673, not considering his inactions in the afternoon. Finally, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber made a second error in paragraph 673; put simply, that his duty to the prisoners expired when the JNA withdrew by 9.00, and he had no further duty to them after that point in time during which they were killed, and in this regard, in this finding, the Trial Chamber legally erred. And finally, Your Honours, I would like to answer your question, number 2 in the addendum. You've asked: Should the Appeals Chamber find that Sljivancanin was under a duty to protect the prisoners of war, pursuant to international humanitarian law, did this duty continue, and on what basis? In our submission, as the person entrusted by Mrksic with the custody and control of the prisoners and with their -- with responsibility for their safety and security, Sljivancanin was obliged under the Laws and Customs of War to protect the prisoners from harm, and this duty to protect the prisoners continued even beyond Mrksic's order to withdraw the JNA. That's our basic proposition, which I'll develop. Mr. Bourgon this morning pointed to a finding of the Trial Chamber - I think it was paragraph 391, if I'm not mistaken - essentially to the effect that his entrusted duty only went so far as Sremska Mitrovica. Your Honours, this is a way-too-narrow reading of the Trial Chamber's findings, and I point you to paragraph 4667 to 668. It is clear from those findings that the entrusted responsibility was not and was not read as narrowly by the Trial Chamber, that he was to be responsible, in fact, for the transport, including the security and safety of the prisoners to their destination, and that's what paragraph 400 says, and that's the Trial Chamber's finding. And I think Your Honour's -- Judge Meron's question about flexibility and a common-sense interpretation must apply here. It couldn't be so fixed that it is simply to Destination A, and if Destination A changes to B, that it could not also include Destination B. And that's clearly the Trial Chamber's finding, that Destination B, i.e., Ovcara, was encompassed within the scope of his entrusted authority. There can be no real question that, as the Trial Chamber found, Sljivancanin was under a duty earlier that day to protect the prisoners of war. If I -- I understand that the Defence does not take issue with the basic proposition that there is a duty to protect prisoners who are in your custody and control. He made that submission more clear this morning. We -- on the first day of this hearing, we did not say that Sljivancanin did not have a duty. In fact, our position is he did have a duty. We acknowledge that it may not have fallen within the normal security organ function to be the repository of being the person who has the control and custody of prisoners. However, in this case he was entrusted specifically by Mrksic with this job, as it were. He had this specifically entrusted on him. Now, to clarify where the duty stems from, the duty, as has been discussed here, stems from Article 13 of the 3rd Geneva Convention, the duty to humanely treat prisoners of war at all times and to protect them from violence and intimidation, and Article 12 of the 3rd Geneva Convention, the duty not to transfer the prisoners of war to a lawless, hostile, and violent party. And we note, Your Honours, that these duties were reflected in the JNA regulations, Exhibit 396, in particular regulation 202 and 210, as well as other applicable JNA guide-lines. In particular, I point Your Honours to Exhibit 856, paragraphs 255 to 261, and Exhibit 581. The Blaskic appeals judgement at paragraph 663 as well as the Oric trial judgement at paragraph 304 have recognised that a failure to discharge such a duty may incur criminal responsibility under Article 7(1), and this indeed accords with the World War II cases that we've heard something of on the first day, where accused were held criminally liable for failing to protect prisoners in their custody and control, including when they permitted prisoners to fall into the hands of others -- other people who harmed them. The real issue in this case is what became of that duty once his specific delegation for the prisoners' custody and control terminated upon the withdrawal of the JNA from Ovcara. In our submission, this duty continued still based on the original sources of his duty; in other words, as a residue of his duties under Articles 12 and 13 of the 3rd Geneva Convention, and I note in this connection that the Defence concedes, in its response brief at paragraph 254, that Article 12 of the 3rd Geneva Convention regarding transfer of prisoners may be relevant by analogy for the transfer of prisoners of war between military authorities within the same armed forces. So I won't develop that particular point right now. Of course, if Your Honours have questions about that, I could try and assist you on that. But our basic proposition, our basic proposition is that a military officer in whom control and custody of prisoners of war is invested must ensure a safe transition for those prisoners, a hand-over to safe custody, even if he is not physically responsible for the transfer. When he learns that they will no longer be humanely treated and that their lives were endangered, he remains under duty to take reasonable steps that are within his power to correct the situation, and allow me, if I may, to develop this a little bit further and to relate it to the present facts. Firstly, Your Honours, we need to consider the nature and scope of his duties under Articles 12 and 13. Now, as I've mentioned, during the afternoon, when Sljivancanin was acting pursuant to his delegated authority over the prisoners, he was under a duty in Article 13 to humanely treat the prisoners of war and ensure they were protected from violence. This is a fundamental guarantee of the Geneva Conventions. In addition, Article 12 required that he be satisfied of the ability and willingness of any transferee party to apply the Geneva Conventions to the prisoners, and based on what he saw and knew about the TOs, a person in Sljivancanin's position could not have been so satisfied, and, again, I am talking about the afternoon or the earlier part of the day. Now, we tie this in. After the prisoners were transferred, that is, after the JNA withdrew by 9.00 p.m., and thereby leaving them in the sole custody of the TOs, these obligations that he had, his obligations under Articles 12 and 13, do not automatically expire. As the person having had custody and control of the prisoners, he continued to have residual duties to them. The fundamental starting point is this: It is a fundamental rule of customary international law that prisoners must at all times be treated humanely and protected from murder and other forms of violence. This is such an axiomatic rule that I hardly need to quote authority on it, but if you look at Rules 87, 89, and 90 of the ICRC, Customary International Law Rules, it confirms this point that I have just made. It is equally clear from the Geneva Conventions and their interpretation in the commentary to those conventions that there cannot be a gap in that protection for prisoners of war and other protected persons, and as the commentary to Article 45 of the 4th Geneva Convention makes clear, when dealing with a very similar provision related to protected persons - we realise that the 4th Geneva Convention applies to civilians, but it's in very similar terms to Article 12 of the 3rd Geneva Convention - and I quote from the commentary to that on page 268: "The power which has transferred the protected persons must not, however, cease to take an interest in their fate. Although they are no longer 'in its hands,' it remains responsible for them insofar as the receiving power fails to fulfill its obligations under the Convention in any important respect, provided that it is notified of such failure by the protecting power." In other words, our submission is that pursuant to the duty under Article 12, the transferor bears a contingent responsibility for the prisoners of war which will be triggered upon learning that the transferee is failing to fulfill its obligations in any important respect. Once the transferor is notified, it's then obliged to take effective measures to correct the situation, or if these measures prove ineffective, it must request the return of the prisoners. This is in the commentary at page 138 to 139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, you are arguing this is -- if I understand you correctly, that this is a situation where there is a conflict between the obligations resulting from the 3rd Geneva Convention and the order of Mrksic to withdraw. So what in this situation is the scope of obligations of Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I will answer your question immediately, Your Honour. In our submission, a member of the military who is in charge of protecting prisoners of war remains under a duty to protect them when he knows that they would otherwise not be protected, and in this case, bringing it back to the facts of this case, it's clear that this contingency was satisfied. Sljivancanin knew that the prisoners would not be humanely treated in accordance with Article 13. Indeed, he knew that the prisoners had been beaten and tortured by the TOs all afternoon. He knows now that their lives are in serious danger if left with this group. At 8.00 p.m., as I've argued previously, he learns that the JNA were leaving, so as Your Honour has said, there is this conflict now between the duties under the 3rd Geneva Convention and this order that he has heard about that Mrksic gave them to leave to Ovcara, and upon learning that, he must have known that this condemned the prisoners to almost certain death, and this is enough, that we say, that should have engaged his responsibility to take effective measures, and I note, Your Honour, that even Sljivancanin himself testified that had he known of the danger the prisoners were to face, he could and should have acted to protect them. That's at transcript page 13751 to 13759. And just to answer the second part of Your Honour's question, and this relates, in fact, to what effective measures he should have taken at this stage, now we acknowledge that what measures, what powers may have been available to him, may have altered, may have changed somewhat, given that he was now no longer -- at that moment that the order was given, he was now no longer acting under Mrksic's specific delegated authority with all of its additional powers and authorities that he was given. However, Your Honours, at least, at the very least, he should have reported through his chain of command -- let's not forgot he's got his parallel reporting structure up to the SSNO. He should have reported the real likelihood that murder would occur if the JNA were to withdraw and the prisoners left in the sole custody of this revengeful group, and yet he took no steps. In that critical hour before the executions began and then throughout that night, he could have done a number of things to reverse their fate. I've already mentioned that he could have reported to General Vasiljevic in the SSNO, and let's not forget, as an addition to that, that detecting and reporting crime was an inherent part of his duties as a security organ. Even he admitted that at transcript 13742, and Exhibit 107 also suggests this. But he didn't even mention it to Vasiljevic. He could have persuaded Mrksic not to withdraw, and again, Your Honours, I point you to JNA regulations paragraph 21, which in fact is a very far-reaching provision of the JNA regulations imposing personal liability on an officer for violations of the laws of war if he knew or could have known not only that units subordinate to him were committing crimes or about to do so, but that other units or individuals were planning the commission of such violations, and if there was still time, it was still possible to prevent their commission. But what did he do? Well, Your Honour used the example of the New York -- is it right that you can go and read "The New York Times." Well, it's not much different here. He went to watch TV. Endorsing the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just to he remind you, you have about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm obliged. Endorsing the Trial Chamber's rigid approach would leave a significant gap in protection for prisoners of war and is inconsistent with the tenor of the protections in Articles 12 and 13 of the 3rd Geneva Conventions. It would subvert the purpose of international humanitarian law if this withdrawal of authority acted like some kind of guillotine to cut off Sljivancanin's duties to the prisoners, and in this case, the injustice of the Trial Chamber's rigid approach is evident. The very act which condemned the prisoners to their ultimate fate, the withdrawal of the JNA, was also the act absolving him of criminal liability. The guarantee of humane treatment for prisoners of war would be rendered nugatory if this finding were allowed to stand. In conclusion, Your Honours, the only reasonable conclusion is that Sljivancanin had a continuing duty to the prisoners throughout that day and night. He could have taken a number of steps in the afternoon before the JNA withdrew, but he did not. Again, in the evening, after he learned of the withdrawal, he could have done a number of things, but he did not. His complete abdication of duty throughout that day and night substantially contributed to the murders, and he was well aware of this. We ask Your Honours to reverse the Trial Chamber's findings and to convict Sljivancanin for aiding and abetting the murders of 194 prisoners at Ovcara, and we submit that the gravity of this crime demands that a sentence of no less than 30 years be imposed. Those complete my submissions. If Your Honours have any further questions, I'd be happy to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I see there are no questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I note the time. I believe we have about five minutes left. Mr. Marwan Dalal will now briefly set out the Prosecution's position on Article 5 and answer Your Honour's question in that regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Dalal, please start.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. As Ms. Brady has just mentioned, I will briefly state the position of the Prosecution with regard to our first ground of appeal relating to entering convictions for crimes against humanity against the accused. Two issues I will mention. First, the issue of the status of the individual victims of Article 5, underlying crimes. The Trial Chamber did not enter a conviction for crimes against humanity against the accused because it found that the victims -- the individual victims in this case did not qualify as civilians, and this was at paragraphs 463 and 481 of the trial judgement. The Prosecution submits that this issue has been resolved by the Martic appeal judgement. The Appeal Chamber in Martic has provided a detailed discussion of the law and concluded that also hors de combat qualify as victims of crimes against humanity, provided, of course, all other conditions of Article 5 are met, and this is at paragraphs 303 to 314 of the Martic appeal judgement. Second, in relation to Your Honour's question or invitation, you've invited the parties to discuss the evidence on the trial record related to; (a), the requirement of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population, especially in relation to the events in Vukovar and, (b), the nexus between the acts of the accused and such an attack. With regard to the widespread and systematic attack portion of your invitation, we refer Your Honours to paragraphs 465 until 472 of the trial judgement. At paragraph 472, the Chamber concluded that: "At the time relevant to the indictment, a widespread and systematic attack by the JNA and other Serb forces directed against the Croat and other non-Serb civilian population in Vukovar and its surrounding indeed took place." We also refer you respectfully to paragraphs 17 to 59 of the trial judgement. With regard to the nexus requirement between the acts of the accused and the widespread and systematic attack, it is also satisfied, in our submission. Both accused were aware of the attack, as they took part in it, starting from October 1991. This is at paragraph 465 of the trial judgement. Objectively, the crimes were part of the attack. The same crimes were committed, also, against civilians by the same group of perpetrators, TO and Serb volunteers, as part of the attack; see, for example, paragraph 47 and Exhibits 312 and 636. The punishment theme is common to the perpetrated crimes and to the widespread and the systematic attack against the civilian population; paragraphs 471, 532, 535, and 510. In addition, both Sljivancanin and Mrksic were aware of the violent and lawless conduct of the TO and volunteers which was directed against civilians and prisoners of war during the attack against Vukovar and its surrounding. This conduct included the killing and brutal treatment of civilians and prisoners of war, as well as looting and other violent and lawless conduct. For Sljivancanin's awareness, see paragraph 664 of the trial judgement. For Mrksic's awareness, see paragraph 621 and reports received by him as commander of the GMTBR within the 1st Military District of the JNA, Exhibits 718, 823, 636, 819, 415, and 847.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Dalal, were any crimes against civilians - I emphasise "civilians" - committed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: In the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, I did not ask about Vukovar. I ask about Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Any crimes against civilians specifically in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Your Honour, to answer specifically your question, a group of victims - and the Trial Chamber left this open - could well have been, indeed, civilians. They were not necessarily -- did not participate in the fighting -- with the Croatian fighting formation in the fighting that took place in Vukovar. So, indeed, at least on this issue, we can say that crimes against civilians were committed in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, the Trial Court was not very clear on that, but let me restate the question. Were any crimes committed at Ovcara aimed at civilians? Do you have any support for that in the trial judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Your Honour, but our submission is that it is not necessary in order to establish the requirement that the crimes were part of the widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You have that with regard to Vukovar, but it has not been quite demonstrated that because of geographical proximity, without more, this is true with regard to Ovcara, and Ovcara, the record would indicate that the crimes were committed, well, almost exclusively, if not exclusively, against POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: But the location is very close to Vukovar, and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: The law does not require that the attack and the crimes be in the same place, as long as we can establish a connection between them, and the connection could be established by the location, by the perpetrators, by the theme that was underlying against the attack and the crimes committed. So the fact that even if we assume for our purposes that at Ovcara crimes against -- attacks against civilians did not intentionally took place, it does it not mean that the crimes in question were not part of the widespread and systematic attack, and I think the law of the Tribunal established that -- establishes that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So, in fact, you are arguing on the basis of proximity alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: No, proximity and perpetrators. The TO and volunteers participated in the attack and committed the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Here we have an attack in Vukovar, which is assumed an attack against the civilian population. A group of POWs, and it would appear only POWs, is transported to Ovcara. There are additional crimes in Ovcara. I would like to see more of a -- sort of a demonstration that this is the same attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: The purpose of my short presentation is for time constraints. In my reply, I can read from exhibits that show that there is a pattern by the same perpetrators during the attack, attacking both civilians and people who were in custody of JNA. I can read from the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. I will not pursue that anymore because there is no time. Have you completed your presentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: For the purposes of this short presentation, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now have a pause, I believe, of 15 minutes, so 5 to 11.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Okay, we will now have response by the counsel for Mr. Mrksic. One hour and thirty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that we will not use up all the time we have at our disposal, so that perhaps the proceedings will be very expeditious today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That is good to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will respond to question number 1 concerning liability under Article 5 of the Statute, and my colleague, Mr. Domazet, will deal with some other issues and circumstances which are important for sentencing. As regards the elements for the existence of a crime against humanity, we submit that all five elements have not been met in this case, as required by international customary law. We must conclude that the Trial Chamber had the task of establishing beyond reasonable doubt that any attack which may have taken place was such that it was primarily directed at the civilian population; further, it had to establish beyond reasonable doubt that there was a nexus between the actions of the accused and the attack on the civilian population, so that the consequences of his action would constitute an objective part of the attack and the accused knew that there was such an attack and that his actions were part of it. After the 18th of November, 1991, on the territory of Vukovar, there were no longer any combat activities or any other activities which might be termed an attack. This can be concluded indirectly from paragraphs 55 and 465 of the judgement which deal with the period from the 18th -- or, rather, from August to the 18th of November, 1991. In paragraph 472 of the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber has in mind a limited period of time, and in the view of the Defence, it follows from this that after the 18th of November, 1991, there were no attacks in this area, especially not attacks directed at the civilian population. These submissions by the Defence are supported by certain exhibits, that is, the report of the EU Monitoring Mission. That's Exhibits 314, 316, 320, 321, and 322; then the reports of the Commission for monitoring the cease-fire, the implementation of the cease-fire, Exhibits 331, 332, 333, 334, and 865; the reports of the Command of Operative Group South, Exhibits 416, 417, 418, and 421; and the reports of the Command of the 1st Military District, Exhibits 423 and 425. The fact that there were no longer any attacks going on is also demonstrated by the presence of the European Union Monitoring Mission, the arrival of the special envoy of the Secretary-General of the UN, Mr. Cyrus Vance, and the negotiations on the implementation of the arrival of peacekeeping forces in this area. Had there been any ongoing attacks at that time, none of these activities would have been undertaken. Although the previous activities in this area, especially in Vukovar, have to be viewed through the lens of the special situation there, reflecting the tactics used by the Croatian armed forces in which President Tudjman introduced his order that civilians, women and children, must not leave Vukovar - that's Exhibit 844 - and throughout these combat activities there were civilians in Vukovar because of this order issued by President Tudjman, and among these civilians was a large number of Serbs, the fact that these operations might have been conducted differently is also indicated by the fact that in the night between the 6th and -- the 16th and 17th of November, the members of the command of the defence of Vukovar were able to leave the town without any fighting or any other problems. After the end of combat activities, there were no further armed activities in the area, but civilians were separated off from persons who had participated in the combat and who were suspected of perpetrating war crimes, and most of the persons falling in this category had gathered in the Vukovar Hospital. As the Trial Chamber established in its judgement, their task was to try to conceal themselves and leave Vukovar together with the convoy of the wounded and civilians, and this can be seen from the testimony of many witnesses, including Vesna Bosanac. The order issued by the Operative Group South Command, that's Exhibit 419, clearly defines what the treatment of civilians, the wounded and the sick should be, and this is mentioned by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 474 of the trial judgement. This column was headed by Colonel Pavkovic, and this convoy reached its destination. Another group of persons separated off by the security organs, in order to be interrogated and either prosecuted or exchanged as suspects suspected of perpetrating war crimes, took a different path, and in paragraph 476 of the trial judgement, we can see the conclusion regarding this separating off. The persons who separated off the potential perpetrators of war crimes from the civilians and wounded in the hospital and those escorting the column and guarding it later on, as well as those who later on perpetrated this crime, were acting under the conviction that their actions were directed against persons who were members of the Croatian armed forces and potential perpetrators of war crimes who had been deprived of their liberty. In part, this conclusion is based by the Trial Chamber -- or, rather, is set out in paragraph 480 of the trial judgement.
