Those acting against these persons acted in the conviction that they were acting against members of the Croatian armed forces. And in paragraphs 480 and 481, the Trial Chamber concludes that no reasonable trier of fact could have concluded that the perpetrator had to know that his actions were aimed against the civilian population of Vukovar. The Defence, therefore, considers that the Trial Chamber concluded rightly that the perpetrators could not have known that there was a systematic and widespread attack on a civilian population because there was no such attack and that it cannot be established that the accused knew that their actions were part of such an attack or that there was a risk that their actions should be part of such an attack. According to the findings of the Trial Chamber, applying Rules 51(A) of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because it included members of various structures of the defence forces of Vukovar, which was proved based on the documentation which was presented here by the Croatian side before the Trial Chamber. These are Exhibits 345, 346, and 554, and my learned friend, Mr. Stephane Bourgon, will be saying more about this. Bearing all this in mind, we submit that no reasonable trier of fact could have found that there was a nexus between the actions of the accused and the attack or, rather, an attack on a civilian population, nor that the actions at Ovcara were part of such an attack, nor that the accused had reason to know that there was such an attack and that their actions could be linked to the activities mentioned by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 472 of the judgement. We therefore consider that there are no elements to establish the liability of the accused Mrksic for the crimes mentioned in Article 5 of the Statute. Your Honours, if you have any questions, I have concluded my part of the arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. So the response -- your response --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I have finished with my section that has to do with Article 5, and now Mr. Domazet will address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Your colleague will speak for roughly how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten to fifteen minutes, not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So I would invite you to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am going to analyse the section that has to do with the sentence, and I'm also going to review some factual matters. The appeal of the OTP contests the decision on the sentence of Mile Mrksic, which they believe to be too mild, not only because the Prosecution considers that the accused should have been pronounced guilty cumulatively, also, from acts of Article 5 of the Statute, but they also consider the sentence overall to be too mild. The Mrksic Defence responded to this appeal with its submissions of the 18th of June, 2008, and especially in paragraphs 56 to 87 of the reply, and it does not wish to reiterate their positions stated in that response. But we will deal with some of the arguments that the Trial Chamber also considered and that are the topic of the Prosecution's appeal. When we are talking about sentencing arguments, according to laws of the former Yugoslavia - this is paragraph 59 of the judgement - it should be said that not only the longest prison sentence provided for that kind of crime in the former Yugoslavia was a sentence of 15 years imprisonment, with the exception of the existence of the death sentence, which was in force at the time, and possibly substituting the death sentence for a 20-year imprisonment, the most important thing is that the aiders and abetters, as is the case here, are sentenced much less severely than the actual perpetrators of the crime or, as is the practice and the terminology here, the articles of joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber did not even differentiate between the punishment for co-perpetrators and the participants of a joint criminal enterprise, which was not established in Mrksic's case, and as pertains to the sentencing for aiding and abetting for which the accused Mrksic was found guilty. I am going to refer now to a generally-known fact, and that is that before the Special Court in Belgrade is at the moment trying a large group of those who are the direct perpetrators of the crime at Ovcara and who were sentenced to a sentence of over 200 years imprisonment altogether, but none of the individual perpetrators were sentenced to a sentence higher than 15 years' imprisonment only because the Court found that that was the maximum sentence provided for under the laws in force at the time. The sentence was quashed for some formal reasons and a retrial is underway, and a judgement is expected to come quite soon, and now the sentences are somewhat higher because some perpetrators in the meantime have been arrested and are being tried with those who were tried in the first trial. When we're talking about the sentence of 20 years pronounced on Mrksic, the Defence will not repeat the arguments that it stated in its appeals submissions, and those are that they believe that the sentence is too severe and too high, and it would be severe even for much more serious charges than the ones that Mrksic was found guilty of, and that is aiding without the desire or intention that these persons be killed. Even if the position of the Prosecution regarding cumulative charging would be accepted for these events, that is, for a larger number of crimes, according to Article 5 of the Statute, the sentence that would reflect the overall conduct of the accused, the participation and attitude towards the executed crime, the sentence passed on my client of 20 years of imprisonment is not too mild; it is actually too severe and too high. First of all, Mile Mrksic was pronounced guilty for aiding and abetting, and according to findings of the Trial Chamber, because of significant practical assistance to members of the TO and the paramilitary, and at the same time the Trial Chamber found that it was not established that Mile Mrksic was guilty of ordering the perpetration of those crimes and that it was not found that he had participated in the joint criminal enterprise, whose common goal would be the perpetration of these crimes. This part of the Trial Chamber's decision was not part of the Prosecution's appeal, but even in spite of that, their appeal does request a higher sentence, and the Mrksic Defence believes that such a request is without grounds and it is untenable because in a real -- realistic review of all the facts presented to the Court would not lead to such a sentence. The Trial Chamber itself established that the sentence cannot be arbitrary or excessive. This is paragraph 683 of the judgement. When talking about the gravity of the crimes, the Trial Chamber states that the sentence must reflect the inherent gravity or the overall punishable conduct of the accused, with due attention being given to the specific circumstances of the case as well as the form and degree of participation of the accused. This is paragraph 684 of the judgement. The correct application of these principles, in view of the fact that Mrksic learned about the endangerment and harassment of the prisoners after the fact, and that beside ordering that security be stepped up as needed, there is no evidence that after that any violence or mistreatment of prisoners occurred until the time after 2235 hours when the paramilitaries and members of the TO who were present started killing them. If because of awareness of this violence upon entering the hangar and the mistreatment of prisoners Mrksic should be held responsible for aiding and abetting, then the sentence for this aiding and abetting would have to be much lower than the one that was passed on him. The Trial Chamber established that in the morning, he omitted to prevent the further commission of crimes of cruel treatment and torture at Ovcara, on which he was informed, and the Trial Chamber finds him responsible on two counts of the indictment. The Trial Chamber established that he was informed by Lieutenant-Colonel Panic and Major Vukasinovic about these facts. According to the positions stated in the judgement, he was informed about this by 5.00 p.m. Vukasinovic did this by 5.00 p.m. However, if Mrksic had not been informed about torture and cruel conduct but only about the fact that the civilians and the TO were endangering the safety of the prisoners, and this had occurred later in the afternoon, sometime by 5.00 p.m., he nevertheless undertook steps so that this would not happen anymore, and the statement of Witness Vezmarovic, the -- whose testimony the Trial Chamber gave credence to, asserts that from the time when he took control with his military police until the end, until he left the hangar, there was no mistreatment or torture of the prisoners or any contact of the paramilitary soldiers or the TO and the prisoners because the TO and the paramilitary members were removed from the hangar. I refer to transcript 8428, from line 8; to 8480; 8498, from line 10; 8501; and 8504. If from that point of time on, which from the transcript seems to be around 5.30 when Vezmarovic took over complete control, no torture or mistreatment of the prisoners actually occurred until the end, and there was no killing either. This is something that this witness is very decisive about. It is clear to the Defence, thus, that the Trial Chamber pronounced the sentence because it found that Mrksic issued the order on the withdrawal of the military police from Ovcara, thus committing aiding and abetting in murder, but Mrksic really did not commit such an act because he never issued such an order to anyone, not even Captain Karanfilov, who did not -- whom he did not see on that day at all, and no evidence was presented on this, that there was any contact between the two of them on that day. The Trial Chamber established, however, that Mrksic conveyed or issued an order directly to Karanfilov. At the time when someone did make this decision and made it possible for happen [as interpreted] what unfortunately did happen, these are the killings at Ovcara, Mrksic was no longer in Negoslavci, and that is why he really cannot bear responsibility for possible aiding or abetting. If his responsibility could have been established for what he found out about the mistreatment at Ovcara, and I repeat, they occurred upon the prisoners' arrival, entry in the hangar, and immediately afterwards, and this is what he was informed about only after the fact and not to the degree that actually happened because what he was informed about by the soldiers was more the actual endangerment and the need for reinforcements rather than telling him fully what the prisoners experienced when they arrived at the hangar and immediately after that. In all of this the Trial Chamber, in the opinion of the Defence, did not evaluate all the mitigating factors and did not evaluate or give proper weight to the impeccable life conduct of Mrksic, professionally and personally; prior to that, his years of service, his family circumstances, and the fact that he voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal as soon as the law on the cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was adopted in Serbia. Especially, they did not take into account his state of health, since he had open-heart surgery and the procedures that that involved during his time here in the Detention Unit of the United Nations. Finally, the Mrksic Defence proposes that if the Appeals Chamber were not to accept the appeal and does not acquit Mrksic of responsibility pursuant to all counts of the indictment and does find that he is guilty for aiding and abetting, either pursuant to all the counts of the indictment on which he was pronounced guilty or only for some of them, we suggest that in that case, he be sentenced to a much lower prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes the response of the Mrksic Defence to the Prosecution appeal. Thank you very much. If you have no additional questions, then we have completed our presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for completing your presentation ahead of time. This means that we will now be able to move on right away to the response by counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. They have altogether one hour and forty-five minutes. They can use now forty-five minutes, and one hour we will use after lunch. I also wanted to draw the attention of the parties, please, and the Registry that since we are likely to complete our hearings today earlier than planned on the amended timetable, I will hold the status conference earlier than envisaged. We will just hold the status conference, say, 10 or 15 minutes after the end of the hearing, simply to enable for tapes to be inserted and so on, but we will not wait until the time I have indicated for the status conference. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will be presenting the first part of our response to the Prosecution appeal, and I will be submitting arguments for Ground number 1, crimes against humanity. And I will, of course, be answering the question that was put forward by the Appeals Chamber, which was suggested to us that we should answer. My colleague will answer -- this afternoon will respond to the second ground of appeal, and, time permitting, we will end our submissions with some remarks on sentencing, which is the third ground of appeal of the Prosecution. Mr. President, I move immediately to the first ground of appeal from the Prosecution dealing with crimes against humanity. As a result of the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Prosecutor v. Martic, the Prosecution normally had two sub-grounds of appeal and has withdrawn its second sub-ground. The second sub-ground was related to the definition of "civilian" in Article 50 of Additional Protocol I and the applicability of that definition to crimes against humanity pursuant to Article 5 of the statute. Accordingly, this morning the Prosecution has limited its arguments to one issue, and that was, namely, whether Article 5 of the Statute requires individual victims to be civilians, and they limited their arguments on this issue to saying that the Appeals Chamber decision in Martic resolves the issue. My submissions this morning will be presented as follows: I will first address the judgement rendered by the Appeals Chamber in the Prosecutor v. Martic, which deals with the same issue as that raised in the Prosecution's first ground of appeal. This will allow me to briefly set out our position in respect of this issue. I will then focus the majority of my submissions this morning to the Appeals Chamber's question related to the evidence on the trial record concerning the requirement of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population and, as the Appeals Chamber put it, especially in relation to the events in Vukovar, and of course the nexus between the acts of the accused and such an attack. Moving on immediately to the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Prosecutor v. Martic, at paragraph 302 of its judgement, the Appeals Chamber found that the definition of "civilian" contained in Article 50 of Additional Protocol I does reflect the definition of "civilian" for the purpose of applying Article 5 of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber also found that the term "civilian," in the context of Article 5 of the Statute, does not include persons hors de combat. Mr. President, this corresponds to one of our main arguments set out in our response brief, and we of course fully agree with both of these findings by the Appeals Chamber, which we maintain are important for the adjudication of this case. That being said, Mr. President, the Appeals Chamber went on to consider, and that is at paragraph 303 of the Appeals Chamber judgement, whether the chapeau of Article 5 of the Statute, namely, that the attack be directed against a civilian population, whether that chapeau also requires that all victims of each individual crime under Article 5 have civilian status. With respect to this issue, the Appeals Chamber concluded at paragraph 307 that there was nothing in the text of Article 5 of the Statute or in previous authorities of the Appeals Chamber which requires that victims of crimes against humanity be civilians. The Appeals Chamber went on to state at paragraph 303 that a person hors de combat may thus be a victim of an act amounting to a crime against humanity, provided, of course, that all other necessary conditions are met; in particular, that the act in question, or the crime, must be part of a widespread or systematic attack against any civilian population. Mr. President, for the reasons set out in the judgement under appeal as further expanded upon in our response brief, we respectfully disagree with this finding of the Appeals Chamber. We submit, as found at paragraphs 102 and 120 of our response, that for the purposes of Article 5 of the Statute, the victims of the underlying crimes must be civilians as defined in Article 51 of Additional Protocol I, which specifically excludes, as we know, soldiers, members of resistance groups, former combatants who have laid down their arms, and/or combatants who are now hors de combat. Consequently, Mr. President, we respectfully ask the Appeals Chamber to revisit its judgement in the Martic case in light of the additional arguments set out in our response. That being said, with a view to focusing on the question put to us by the Appeals Chamber this morning, we will not expand further on this issue, and I will move right away to that question. The question was at follows: First of all, the question takes, as a premise, that the Appeals Chamber judgement in Martic will hold; namely, that a person hors de combat may be a victim of a crime against humanity, provided that all other necessary conditions are met, and in particular that the act in question be part of a widespread or systematic attack against any civilian population. In answering the Appeals Chamber question, I will first set out what our position is as to whether the chapeau requirement for Article 5 is met in this case. I will then expand on the underlying legal principles which must be considered, and I will follow by highlighting the evidence on the record which supports our position. Our position, Mr. President, can be summarised as follows: Firstly, on 20 November 1991, when crimes were committed at Ovcara by members of the TO and paramilitaries, there was no widespread and systematic attack directed on the civilian population on that day. Accordingly, in our view, this is sufficient for the chapeau requirements not to be met and for the verdict of acquittal, which was returned by the Trial Chamber for Counts 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6, to stand. Secondly, should the Appeals Chamber hold on the basis of the evidence on the record that there was a widespread or systematic attack directed at the civilian population on 20 November 1991, then we say that the acts committed by the perpetrators were not part of the widespread and systematic attack directed at the civilian population on that day and, of course, that there was no nexus between the acts committed by the perpetrators and this attack. Consequently, the chapeau requirements of Article 5 would not be met, and once again, this would justify that the verdict of acquittal returned by the Trial Chamber for Counts 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 to stand. Finally, Mr. President, the third step, should the Appeals Chamber hold on the basis of the evidence in this case on the record that there was a widespread or systematic attack directed at the civilian population and that there was the necessary nexus between the acts of the perpetrators and this attack, then it is our submission that the perpetrators either did not know that their acts constituted part of a pattern of widespread or systematic crimes directed at a civilian population, nor did they know that their acts fitted into such a pattern. Consequently, the mens rea requirement, pursuant to Article 5 of the statute, would not be met, and once again, the verdict of acquittal returned by the Trial Chamber for these counts should stand. In this regard, Mr. President, it is our submission that the mens rea requirement must also be assessed in this case from the point of view of Mr. Sljivancanin as well as from the point of view of the perpetrators. I now move on, Mr. President, to setting out briefly the legal principles which form the basis of our position in this case. Firstly, we believe that the first legal consideration of importance is to understand the difference which exists between the following notions: Armed conflict; attack pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute; attack pursuant to Article 49(1) of Additional Protocol I; and unlawful attack against a civilian population pursuant to Articles 51(2) and 85(3)(A) of Additional Protocol I. In this regard, it is well known that pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute of this Tribunal, a requirement exists exceptionally that a crime against humanity be committed in armed conflict, whether international or non-international. Moreover, pursuant to the case law of the International Tribunal, we know that an armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between states or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a state. I refer to Tadic, paragraph 407, the jurisdiction decision of 2 October 1995, paragraph 70. As for an attack within the meaning of Article 5 of the Statute, it has been defined as a course of conduct involving acts of violence, and it is not limited to the use of armed force, and it may also encompass any mistreatment of the civilian population. This is found in Kunarac Appeals Chamber judgement, paragraph 86. In this regard, it follows, Mr. President, that the concept of armed conflict and the concept of attack, pursuant to Article 5, are not identical; Tadic Appeals Chamber judgement, paragraph 251. The two must be separate notions, although, of course, under Article 5 of the Statute the attack against any civilian population may be part of an armed conflict; Kunarac Appeals Chamber decision, paragraph 86. Moving on quickly, Mr. President, to the definition of attack for IHL purposes, pursuant to international humanitarian law. Article 49(1) defines "attack" as acts of violence against the adversary, whether in offence or defence. In other words, "attack," pursuant to Additional Protocol I, refers to the use of armed force by one party against another, which of course will be his adversary. The final notion that we need to address is that of unlawful attack on a civilian population pursuant to the Laws of War and as defined by reference to Articles 51(2) and 85(3) of Additional Protocol I. In accordance with these provisions, the term "unlawful attack" on a civilian population refers to an attack, as defined pursuant to Article 49(1) of Additional Protocol I, which is unlawful because it is directed at a civilian population as defined in Article 51(2), and of course which results in civilian death, and that is as held by the Appeals Chamber in the Prosecutor v. Kordic at paragraph 67. From these definitions, Mr. President, it is possible to conclude the following: Firstly, an attack pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute does not necessarily involve an attack pursuant to Article 49(1) of Additional Protocol I. In this regard, an attack may happen during an armed conflict, and it may also -- and the attack against -- the Article 5 attack, sorry, may happen during an armed conflict, and it may also out-last the armed conflict. Secondly, the term "armed conflict" may but does not necessarily involve an attack pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute. Thirdly, an armed conflict will most likely involve attacks, as defined pursuant to the Laws of War, Article 49(1) of the Additional Protocol I, but the presence of attacks, pursuant to Article 49(1), may very well be happening without there being an attack pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute. Putting all these notions together will be important when we assess the facts and the evidence on the record in this case. The second legal consideration which is, in our submission, important is the meaning to be given to "directed against," in the context of Article 5 of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber has clarified that this term, "directed against," is an expression which specifies that in the context of a crime against humanity, the civilian population is the primary object of the attack. What is significant here are the criteria which the Appeals Chamber has identified in order that if we consider these criteria, we will be able to determine whether there was, indeed, an attack directed against the civilian population, and these include the means and methods used in the course of the attack; the status of the victim - very important; the number of victims; the discriminatory nature of the attack; the nature of the crimes committed during the attack; the resistance to the assailants at the time; the extent to which the attacking force may be said to have complied or attempted to comply with the precautionary requirements pursuant to the Laws of War; and finally, to the extent that the alleged crimes against humanity were committed during the course of an armed conflict, that the Laws of War, of course, provide a benchmark against which the nature of the attack and the legality of the acts committed can be assessed. This will be, again, also important when we assess the evidence on the record. The third legal consideration which is of importance, in our submission, is the meaning to be given to "widespread and systematic." In our view, however, these terms are well defined in the case law of the International Tribunal, and there's no need to further expand on them at this point. The last legal consideration which is of importance, in our submission, is the meaning to be given to Article 5 of the Statute, the requirement that the acts of the perpetrator must constitute part of the attack. The Appeals Chamber in Kunarac has confirmed that this refers to the nexus which must exist between the acts of the accused and the attack. The Appeals Chamber has also said that the required nexus comprises two elements; firstly, the acts committed which by its nature and its consequence is objectively part of the attack; and, secondly, the accused must know that there is an attack directed at the civilian population and that his acts are part of it. With respect to the first element, as part of, namely, the commission of an act which by its nature and consequences is objectively part of the attack, the Appeals Chamber has held that the acts need not be committed in the midst of the attack, but it must be sufficiently connected to be part of the attack. The Appeals Chamber has also held that the crime must not be an isolated act. Consequently, Mr. President, in our submission, the following must be looked at to determine whether the crime is part of the attack: The nature of the crime, the consequences of the crime, the context and the circumstances in which the crime was committed, and the connection between the crime and the attack. As for the second element of the term "as part of," it requires two things. The accused must know that there is an attack directed at the civilian population, and he must know that his acts are part of that attack against the civilian population. This knowledge, of course, is part of the mens rea requirement for crimes against humanity. Even though it is not necessary for the accused to have knowledge of the details of the attack itself, the attack which was directed at the civilian population, evidently the accused must have known the nature and the consequences of the attack directed against the civilian population. And, more particularly, what is of critical importance, that the target victim group comprises civilians as defined in Article 51 of Additional Protocol I. Why is this so important? Simply because when the time comes to determine whether the accused knew that his crime was part of the attack against the civilian population, it will be necessary to compare the knowledge -- his knowledge of the target group of his crime and his knowledge with the target group of the attack against the civilian population. It will also be necessary to compare the knowledge of the accused regarding the consequences of his acts, meaning his crimes, with the knowledge -- his knowledge of the consequences of the attack against the civilian population. Having looked at the legal considerations which are of importance to support our submission, we can now move on to the exact questions which were put to us by the Appeals Chamber. Of course, the first question, which is not included, is: Was there an armed conflict on 20 November 1991? The Trial Chamber held, and that is at paragraph 422, that an armed conflict existed in the broader area of the municipality of Vukovar and elsewhere in Croatia, which commenced by the end August 1991 and continued until after the events charged in the indictment. Accordingly, it is not disputed in this appeal that there was an armed conflict on 20 November 1991, but the most -- the more important question: Was there on 20 November 1991 a widespread or systematic attack directed at the civilian population of Vukovar? And to answer this question, we must first look at the events up to 18 November based on the Trial Chamber's findings. The Trial Chamber found - paragraph 465 - that from 23 August until 18 November, the town of Vukovar and its surroundings were increasingly subjected to shelling and other fire, and the damage to the city was devastating. The siege of Vukovar commenced on 25 August 1991; that is paragraph 37. At paragraph 465, in essence, the city of Vukovar was encircled and under siege until the Croat forces capitulated on 18 November. I also refer to the following findings of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 468, where the battle of Vukovar caused a large number of casualties, both dead and wounded, combatants and civilians, and the Chamber accepted as a reliable estimate that the casualties were 60 to 75 per cent civilian; paragraph 466, that the buildings were shelled, including schools, kindergartens, and wells were also targeted and destroyed; paragraph 470, that the attack consciously and deliberately directed against the city of Vukovar itself and its helpless civilian population, trapped as they were by the military blockade of Vukovar; paragraph 472, the extensive damage to civilian property and civilian infrastructure, the number of civilians killed or wounded during the military operations, and the high number of civilians forced to flee, clearly indicate that the attack was carried out in an indiscriminate way, contrary to international law. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber found that at the time relevant to the indictment, there was in fact not only a military operation against the Croat forces in and around Vukovar but also a widespread and systematic attack by the JNA and other Serb forces directed at the Croat and other non-Serb civilian population in the wider Vukovar area; 472, trial judgement. On the basis of this evidence, Mr. President, the following conclusions can be drawn: Firstly, that from late August 1991 until 18 November, there was an unlawful attack against the civilian population, pursuant to the Laws of War and Article 51(2) and 52(1) of Additional Protocol I; secondly, in parallel to this attack, in the same period there was a widespread and systematic attack directed against the civilian population pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute; and, thirdly, according to the Trial Chamber, the acts of violence and the unlawful acts which constituted the unlawful attack against the civilian population and civilian objects, pursuant to the Laws of War or Additional Protocol I, are the same acts of violence and unlawful acts which it qualified as a widespread or systematic attack directed against the civilian population. That being said, we now turn to the period what happens between the 18th of November and the 20th of November. Once again, a two-step process is required. First, we need to look at the findings of the Trial Chamber. It found that the Croatian forces in and around Vukovar capitulated on 18 November, but on 18 November, 4.000 civilians took steps to leave Vukovar and that their evacuation was assisted by the JNA; paragraph 157. At paragraphs 130 to 144, the Zagreb Agreement is discussed. The Zagreb Agreement was reached on 18 November, agreement on a humanitarian convoy to evacuate the wounded and the sick from the Vukovar Hospital, as well as a cease-fire in the area of Vukovar Hospital and along the agreed evacuation route. Preparation for the evacuation of the hospital was done between 18 to 20 November - that's paragraphs 180 to 189 of the trial judgement - and on 20 November at 700 hours in the morning, the beginning of the evacuation of the hospital, at paragraph 199. We also need to look at the following evidence on the record, and we respectfully refer the Trial Chamber to the following exhibits: 368, 417, 418, 419, 421, 425, 734, and 735. These exhibits, Mr. President, are combat reports submitted by Operation Group South to the command of the 1st Military District Command, as well as from the 1st Military District Command to the Operations Centre of the SFRY, and these combat reports cover the period from 18 to 22 November. We also respectfully refer the Appeals Chamber to Exhibits 314, 315, 316, 320, 321, 322, 323, 333, 334, 339, 340, 341, and 344. These are reports prepared by the European Community [sic] Monitoring Mission during the period from 16 to 27 November 1991. And of course, we also refer the Appeals Chamber to Exhibit 40, which is the Zagreb Agreement, which is a document setting out the agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Yugoslav People's Army, the International Committee of the Red Cross, Medecins Sans Frontieres, as well as the Maltese Cross. This agreement regarding the convoy to evacuate the wounded and sick from the Vukovar Hospital refers to the evacuation of 20 November, and it includes, among other things, an undertaking by both parties, Croatia and the Yugoslav People's Army, to guarantee a cease-fire in the area of Vukovar Hospital and along the evacuation route. Mr. President, it is our submission that these documents establish amongst other things the ongoing efforts and the intent of the Yugoslav People's Army during this period to organise the evacuation of civilians, to evacuate the wounded and sick, and to care for the civilian population. These documents also establish that there is no more shelling and no more offensive operations, although there are, according to the reports, a few skirmishes where Croat forces refused to surrender. Consequently, it is our submission on the basis of this evidence, including the exhibits referred to and the findings of the Trial Chamber, and of course bearing in mind the criteria mentioned earlier, which must be considered to determine whether there is a widespread or systematic attack directed at the civilian population, and our submission is that the unlawful attack against the civilian population, pursuant to Additional Protocol I, ended on 18 November with the surrender of the Croat forces. Also, the widespread and systematic attack directed against the civilian population, pursuant to Article 5, also ended on 18 November 1991, as evidenced by the fact that there was no longer any course of conduct involving the commission of acts of violence directed at the civilian population, and, of course, there was no longer any course -- any mistreatment of the civilian population. In other words, Mr. President, during the period from 18 to 20 November, there has been a complete change in the situation, which has evolved from fighting using armed force between the Yugoslav People's Army and Croatian forces to a situation where both parties and, more importantly, the Yugoslav People's Army, displayed the will to protect the civilian population and not to hurt or mistreat the civilian population in any way. We're talking about, of course, humanitarian efforts. On this basis, we respectfully submit that on 20 November, there was no widespread or systematic attack directed at the civilian population in the Vukovar area, and that for this reason, the chapeau requirements of Article 5 was not met. What is significant here, Mr. President, is the parallel that was established by the Trial Chamber between the unlawful attack pursuant to the Laws of War and the widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute. The evidence makes it clear that both of them ended on 18 November 1991. The third question which needs to be addressed is the following: Were the unlawful acts committed at Ovcara on 20 November part of any widespread or systematic attack directed at the civilian population which ended on 18 November 1991? Based on the evidence on the record, the answer to that question, Mr. President, is a definite no. According to the Prosecution, a sufficient nexus exists between the events at Ovcara because it happened two days after the end of the surrender, in the same geographical area, and because it was committed by persons who were involved in the fighting or the same persons who were involved in the fighting, persons who would -- who harboured feelings of animosity towards enemy Croatian forces. It is our submission, Mr. President, that this is not sufficient to establish the necessary nexus. As we have seen earlier, the nexus comprises two elements; firstly, the acts at Ovcara must be objectively part of the attack - of course, the Article 5 attack - by their nature and consequences; and the accused must know that the crimes are part of the attack directed at the civilian population. Assessing the first of these elements on the basis of the evidence on the record, we find the following: Firstly, the nature of the crime, the torture of prisoners of war at Ovcara, is entirely different. During the fighting, before 18 November, the use of armed force was directed indiscriminately at the civilian population and the civilian infrastructure. Vukovar was under siege, and the fighting against the Croatian forces at that moment was legitimate. Looking at the consequences of the crime, they are completely different. The victims at Ovcara were exclusively prisoners of war, while the victims of the widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population before 18 November were primarily and mostly civilians, and the consequence was devastation of the civilian infrastructure. Looking at the context and the circumstances in which the crimes at Ovcara were committed, they have no connection with the unlawful attack against the civilian population at the time when Vukovar was under siege. Active fighting was taking place between parties to the conflict, and the Croatian forces had not yet surrendered. At Ovcara, prisoners of war were detained and mistreated, there was no more fighting, and the Yugoslav People's Army was focusing all of its efforts on the evacuation and the care of civilians. As a matter of fact, a clear distinction can be established between the unlawful acts of the TOs and paramilitaries and even the acts and intent of the JNA forces at the same moment. Consequently, the crimes of the TOs and paramilitaries at Ovcara exclusively against prisoners of war were not directed at the civilian population of Vukovar. Assessing the second element on the basis of evidence, we find the following: Firstly, it can be said on the basis of the evidence that the perpetrators of the mistreatment at Ovcara were aware of the widespread or systematic attack directed against the civilian population up to 18 November. That being said, they knew that both the unlawful attack against the civilian population pursuant to the Laws of War, the shelling and so, as well as the widespread and systematic attack directed against the civilian population, pursuant to Article 5, both of them ended on 18 November, and the perpetrators knew this, and they knew that the focus of the JNA after that date was the evacuation and the care of both civilians and the sick and wounded. The real question, then, is whether they knew that their crimes, the crimes they committed, were part of the Article 5 attack. The following findings of the Trial Chamber are important in this regard: The persons removed by the JNA forces from the Vukovar Hospital on 20 November and taken to Ovcara, there by Serb forces, had been specifically identified, being that they were known or were believed to have been active in the Croatian forces; paragraph 480. They were identified and taken into JNA custody as prisoners of war; same paragraph, 480. The perpetrators of the offence against the prisoners of war on 20-21 November acted in the understanding that their acts were directed against members of the Croatian forces, not against the civilian population. The members of the Serb forces who had custody of the victims on 20 November and those who executed them that evening and night at Ovcara acted in the knowledge and belief that the victims were prisoners of war, not civilians, as well as in the understanding that their acts were directed against the members of Croatian forces; paragraphs 480, 481. On the basis of these findings, Mr. President, here's what we have to look at: We have two things. First, we have to look at the knowledge of members of the TOs and paramilitaries concerning the widespread and systematic attack before the 18th of November; then, the knowledge and the understanding of members of the TOs and paramilitaries concerning their own crimes on 20 November. As mentioned earlier, this comparison must take place on the basis of the consequences, the context, the circumstances, and the connection, if any, between the crimes in both cases. Consequently, on this basis, on the basis of the totality of the evidence on the record, there's only one possible conclusion, and that is, Mr. President, that the members of the TOs and the paramilitaries who committed crimes at Ovcara on 20 November were not aware that these crimes fit in or were part of the widespread or systematic attack which -- directed at the civilian population of Vukovar, which ended on 18 November 1991. Lastly, Mr. President, it is necessary to look at these events from the point of view of Mr. Sljivancanin. Is it reasonable to think that Mr. Sljivancanin knew that the mistreatment of the prisoners of war at Ovcara, considering the nature, the consequences, as well as the context and the circumstances in which crimes were committed, is it reasonable to think that he knew that this was part of the widespread or systematic attack directed at the civilian population which ended on 18 November? Of course not, Mr. President. According to the Trial Chamber, Mr. Sljivancanin was entrusted by his commander to organise the evacuation of the civilians at the Vukovar Hospital, including the triage operation, to ensure that members of the Croatian forces would be dealt with in accordance with the law. With the help of others, he personally screened and made sure that to the best his knowledge no members of the Croatian forces would evade their responsibility as potential war criminals by being evacuated with the civilians he was caring for and no civilians would face legal proceedings along with members of the Croatian forces who were now prisoners of war. At one point, when 12 to 15 persons were returned from the JNA barracks to the hospital, to the Vukovar Hospital, he did not hesitate to review his own prior decisions to ensure that this was so. Some of them were put with the civilians who were evacuated; others were returned to the JNA barracks where they pursued with the prisoners of war. And although we maintain that he was never at Ovcara, if the Appeals Chamber holds that he did go there and that he did see any mistreatment, there was certainly no doubt in his mind that prisoners of war were being mistreated and not civilians, by members of the TO and the paramilitaries who at that time did not agree nor act in accordance with the humanitarian efforts of the Yugoslav People's Army, that this was unrelated to the widespread or systematic attack directed at the civilian population of Vukovar which ended on 18 November. For all these reasons, Mr. President, we respectfully request the Appeals Chamber to dismiss the Prosecution's ground of appeal and confirm the verdict of acquittal returned by the Trial Chamber for Counts 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6. Respectfully submitted, Mr. President.
