utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. So if I'm not mistaken, the counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin has another up to 60 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I would now like to provide argumentation of the Defence that has to do with our response to the second ground of appeal of the OTP. The essence of it is in the alleged error of the Court in paragraph 672 of the judgement. That is the core of the matter. According to the Prosecutor, no reasonable trier of fact would come to the conclusion that the Trial Chamber came to; namely, that Sljivancanin had reason to believe that members of the Territorial Defence and the paramilitaries would not attempt murder because then it was the Yugoslav People's Army that was providing security for the prisoners. That is paragraph 99 of the appeal. Its argumentation is based on the previous knowledge of Sljivancanin about the actions of the TO and the paramilitaries, as well as his awareness of the JNA not preventing these persons from committing crimes in the previous period. That is what the OTP says. The OTP, lacking argumentation concerning this alleged error made by the Trial Chamber, actually extensively repeats the conclusions and findings of the Court on the evidence provided that should show that Sljivancanin was aware of the behaviour of the members of the TO as persons who are capable of committing murder. All assertions made by the Prosecutor on Sljivancanin's awareness of previous crimes of members of the TO and paramilitaries were something that the Trial Chamber did have in mind when they found what they did in paragraph 672, and they unequivocally said that, stating: It is true that Sljivancanin must have been aware on the basis of his knowledge of the events at Velepromet on the 19th of November, 1991, that at least some of the TOs and paramilitaries were capable of killing. However, what the Trial Chamber established as a key fact in its findings as to why Sljivancanin could have assumed there would be no killings was the presence of the security of the JNA. The Prosecutor did not show that the Trial Chamber erred in those findings that led to a miscarriage of justice. The Prosecutor did not challenge the key findings of the Trial Chamber from the judgement, which had as a direct consequence this consequential conclusion from paragraph 672 that we are discussing. In actual fact, the Trial Chamber, in paragraphs 620 and 621, concluded that the danger came to be, in terms of the lives of the prisoners in the hangar, after the JNA security withdrew. The Prosecution did not challenge the evidence that the Trial Chamber refers to. Evidence actually shows that the killings were committed after the military security withdrew; paragraphs 252 and 294. It is clear that the JNA and the members of the security of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade were actually between the immediate perpetrators of the crimes of murder and the victims. The Trial Chamber did not establish that the killings occurred in the period while there was security provided by the JNA at Ovcara; paragraphs 494 and 508. That was also not challenged by the Prosecution in their appeal. Had the Trial Chamber concluded on the basis of the evidence adduced that there was a danger for the lives of prisoners even at the time when the JNA was providing security at Ovcara and that this danger had as a direct consequence a direct attack against the lives of prisoners, then there could be a connection established between possible previous knowledge of Sljivancanin about the proneness of members of the TO in terms of committing crimes and possible incapacity to provide security in order to prevent killings from taking place. In contrast to that construction made by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber established that the killings started after 2100 hours, that is to say, after the security withdrew. The military police of the 80th Brigade was that buffer in whose presence the members of the TO could not jeopardise the lives of the prisoners on that afternoon. The Prosecutor himself in paragraph 186 claims that the withdrawal of the security of the JNA from Ovcara left the prisoners in the hands of the TO and the paramilitaries, who then killed them over several hours. Then, in paragraph 199 of their appeal, the OTP says that the order on the withdrawal of security after 2100 hours, the prisoners remained in the hands of the TO and the paramilitaries, and that then they: [In English] "... vented their desire for revenge without restraint." [Interpretation] And they refer to paragraph 620 of the judgement as a reference for this assertion. And in that paragraph that the Prosecutor refers to, the Trial Chamber, in relation to the consequences of the withdrawal of security, says the withdrawal of the JNA guards removed this one restraint. What followed dramatically demonstrates that the JNA guards had been effective, and the gravity and intensity of the hatred and desire for revenge was then able to be unleashed without restraint. It is not only that the OTP does not challenge these findings of the Trial Chamber, but as a matter of fact they support it, and in their own appeal, in their third ground, they refer to it. The Prosecutor supported this same thesis two days ago - transcript reference 7317 - when Mr. Rogers said, in relation to Mr. Mrksic: [In English] "He ordered the withdrawal of 80th Motorised Brigade, the only protective force keeping the killers at bay." [Interpretation] And then on page 87, line 11, he also says: [In English] "When he did act, it was to withdraw the only security they had and to consign them to their fate." [Interpretation] In the judgement, the Trial Chamber concluded that Sljivancanin, on the basis of his prior knowledge on their behaviour during the events in Ovcara, had to be aware that some of them might commit crimes, including murders. The Defence, in their response in paragraphs 188 through 198, and also in our appeal, paragraph 441 to 467 inclusive, dealt in detail with the argumentation in which we challenged the findings of the Court in terms of this element of Sljivancanin's mens rea. In his appeal, the Prosecutor, in support of these findings of the Court, provides some evidence that would corroborate that. He bases Sljivancanin's prior knowledge on written reports prior to the 18th of November, 1991, his emphasis on the necessity of prevention of any kind of conflict with the prisoners who were handed over on the 18th of November, that is to say, two days prior to what had happened, then information on the events in Velepromet obtained from Colonel Vujic, his knowledge about what happened in the barracks and events in Ovcara during his alleged stay there, and his alleged knowledge on the withdrawal of the security. In relation to these points made by the Prosecution, we wish to remind you, first and foremost, that the Sljivancanin Defence asserts that Sljivancanin was not in Ovcara, was not in the barracks, was not informed by Vujic about the events in Velepromet, and that he did not have knowledge on the withdrawal of security. We presented our arguments about that in detail in various paragraphs in our reply. If the Honourable Appeals Chamber accepts any one of these assertions made by the Defence, then the thesis on his previous knowledge concerning the behaviour of members of the TO is untenable. Also, even if you were to accept the findings of the Trial Chamber in this regard, Your Honours, this should not at all change the conclusion of the Trial Chamber that Sljivancanin, as stated in paragraphs 672 of the statement [as interpreted], reasonably -- could have reasonably believed in the circumstances that the TOs and the paramilitaries would be unlikely to resort to killing. Just a moment, please. What I've said here, it's not "statement." It should say "judgement." I see that there is an error in the transcript. We wish to point out that the Prosecutor says that Sljivancanin's concern that there would be a clash between the members of the JNA and the first group of prisoners on the 18th of November and that they base their complaint on that, and it was Karanfilov and then the security followed, so if Sljivancanin had reason for a concern, this concern not to have any kind of conflict occur, then it has to be established what it was that actually happened because that also constitutes Sljivancanin's awareness of the possibility of killings in Ovcara on the 20th of November and the functioning of the JNA. On the 18th of November, everything functioned impeccably. On the next morning, the prisoners were transferred from Ovcara to the Mitrovica prison without any incidents whatsoever. We wish to point out that this is the same security, at the same place, with the same group of prisoners, roughly, like two days later, when the crime that you are dealing with here today actually occurred. After this security provided on the 18th of November, Sljivancanin only could have been aware that there was no danger of a conflict and that the members of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade were, indeed, possible of providing security in that facility for such a large number of prisoners. Also, according to the judgement, the members of the JNA prevented the entry of members of the TO and paramilitaries in the area of the hospital on the 19th of November. That is paragraph 184. Then the crimes that the Trial Chamber established had taken place in Velepromet, if they're not viewed as an isolated incident, but within the context of the sources of knowledge as to whether it could have reasonably been assumed that killings would occur at Ovcara, this leads to a completely different conclusion from that that is drawn by the Prosecutor. The members of the JNA in Velepromet prevented crimes through their activities. Obviously, in that facility that was under the Territorial Defence, when a large number of civilians arrived on the 19th of November, 1991, there was confusion and crimes did take place. Obviously, like in the first moments when the prisoners arrived in the barracks and at Ovcara on the 20th of November, the present members of the JNA at first did not react appropriately. However, that cannot be a conclusion that would indicate the passivity of the JNA in relation to possible killings. It can clearly be established from the findings of the Court that through any activity of the members of the JNA -- that all activities of the members of the JNA led to the withdrawal of TO members or, rather, that they refrained from any further assaults. This is indicated in the findings of the Trial Chamber in several paragraphs in relation to Velepromet; for example, when a JNA officer appeared, the attacks against the prisoners stopped; that's paragraph 163. When another officer of the JNA arrived, he took the members of the Territorial Defence away and they did not -- they could no longer attack Witness Vujic. That is paragraph 171. That means that the bus managed to leave when the JNA intervened without further obstruction. Then in the evening hours, certain prisoners were transferred to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica with the guards of the JNA; paragraph 168. There was an identical situation at the barracks. The attacks of the TO and paramilitaries and the alleged passive behaviour of the JNA in barracks at first could not be viewed in an isolated manner. This is most tellingly demonstrated by the -- by paragraph 216 of the judgement that the OTP does not challenge; that is to say, that 30 minutes after the bus arrived in the barracks, there was order established when the military policemen of the JNA removed the members of the TO and the paramilitary forces from the compound of the barracks. The Prosecution witnesses, prisoners from the bus, testified, stating that JNA soldiers did not allow anyone to enter the bus, and this was testified to by P-012 on page 3732; Dodaj, page 5598; then Witness Karlovic, then Witness P-030, page 9741. Karlovic confirmed that at that moment while he was on the bus, he felt safe, since JNA security was there; that is transcript reference 6335. Witness Berghofer said that he was not mistreated in the barracks, and the conclusion of the Trial Chamber, in paragraph 216, supports this testimony. It is clear that the JNA, through its efficient action, managed to remove the members of the TO and paramilitaries from the bus and the barracks and to establish full control over their security. This is the information that Sljivancanin received from Vukasinovic, his deputy, and that the Trial Chamber refers to in paragraph 374 of the judgement. The same conclusions have to be made in relation to the events in Ovcara during the course of the afternoon. Although the security at first did not react in an appropriate manner, the further sequence of events and conclusions of the Trial Chamber show that the security was effective and efficient in relation to the lives of the prisoners, protecting the lives. I would like to underline that. When Captain Vezmarovic arrived, the commander of the military police or the brigade that provided security for the hangar, all persons except for the prisoners and security were removed from the hangar. The Trial Chamber says in paragraph 265: It was only members of the military police that remained in the hangar. The witness Vezmarovic testified himself, and my colleague Mr. Domazet also referred to his testimony, and we consider that to be very important; namely, that through his orders, he fully established control in the hangar - transcript reference 8421, line 19 - and that is when, in his view, the security started functioning in a normal manner, and then he repeated again that from then onwards, the situation was under control; 8568, line 15 is the transcript reference. The conclusions of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 620 that we already mentioned is unequivocal -- are unequivocal. This paragraph states the JNA was, in the main, a disciplined military force with a strong leadership. Then, it says, the presence of JNA guards at Ovcara that day had provided effective restraint against the members of the TO and paramilitary forces. And, finally, fundamentally in relation to the topic that we are discussing, the withdrawal from Ovcara of the only remaining JNA soldiers guarding the prisoners of war had an immediate and direct effect on the commission of the murders that followed. This thesis, expounded in the judgement, is fully supported by the OTP because they refer to it in their own appeal, as we've already said at the very beginning. The Prosecutor cannot consider some findings from the judgement good in the case of one accused person and bad in the case of another person; the very same findings, that is. The Prosecution did not challenge the findings of the Court that are directly related to that paragraph, and I'm referring to paragraph 658. The Trial Chamber says, at the most, he could have been aware that crimes might be committed if the TOs and paramilitaries were allowed access to the prisoners of war without proper security, and that's what I underline, "without property security." The OTP did not challenge those findings of the Trial Chamber either. I wish to conclude this part of my remarks. Not through a single one of their arguments did the OTP show that the Trial Chamber erred when they established, in paragraph 672 of the statement, that Sljivancanin reasonably could have believed in the circumstances that the TOs and paramilitary would be unlikely to resort to killing. On the contrary, through their arguments, the OTP, and supporting the findings of the Trial Chamber from paragraph 620, showed themselves how right these findings of the Trial Chamber were. As I continue, I'm going to present our position in relation to question number 3. The question of the Appeals Chamber was: What is our position about the time when Sljivancanin found out about Mrksic's order to withdraw? Our response is simple. Sljivancanin at no point during the relevant period in the indictment did not find out about the decision to withdraw security from Ovcara. This position of the Defence was accepted by the Trial Chamber in its judgement. The Chamber specifically, in its findings in paragraph 661, provided all arguments which counter the construction of the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber established, I quote: "There is no indication in the evidence that Veselin Sljivancanin was at Negoslavci at the time the order was first given by Mile Mrksic." He could have been informed by other means, but this is merely conjecture. The Prosecution does not dispute in its appeal the assertions from paragraph 661 of the judgement. This entire paragraph speaks about the findings of the Trial Chamber, which completely differently evaluate evidence from the current attempt by the Prosecution. The Prosecution now, especially in its reply, is doing what -- is constantly repeating that it is unacceptable to do something in the appeals procedure, and that is to make its own evaluation and interpretation of the findings of the Trial Chamber which are contrary to those same findings. All the arguments of the Prosecutor are practically an attempt to take the conclusion about the knowledge of Sljivancanin or awareness about the withdrawal of the security be derived from an additional or subsequent assessment of the evidence that has already been evaluated. The Prosecution is trying to base its assertions on the fact that it will draw its conclusions on the basis of indirect evidence and conclusions of the Trial Chamber that talk about completely different facts, and thus, they claim that Sljivancanin had to have known about the decision to withdraw the security, because -- so this is something that cannot be substantiated in the findings of the Trial Chamber. The Defence asserts that his knowledge should be based on his duties to the prisoners and not about when the security was withdrawn. That is why the Trial Chamber has found that Sljivancanin's responsibility stopped with the withdrawal of the security detail. So the position of the Defence is that that finding of the Trial Chamber cannot substantiate the assertions of the Prosecution. Thus, the Trial Chamber established when his duty towards the prisoners of war stopped and not whether he knew about the withdrawal. The Prosecutor said that Sljivancanin found out about the withdrawal of the security that evening at Negoslavci when he returned there, but Vukasinovic, as he testified, or Borisavljevic, neither of them testified that at that time when they were in touch with Vukasinovic and Sljivancanin was it known that the security was withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no conversations that the security was withdrawing, and there was nothing to indicate that there was information that they were aware, either of them, that the security was withdrawing. Vukasinovic and Sljivancanin both testified that Vukasinovic told Sljivancanin only what was happening at Ovcara during the time he was there, about which Mrksic was subsequently informed as well. The Trial Chamber established that it would be pure conjecture that Sljivancanin found out about the decision of the withdrawal not when it was reached, but also in any other way, and the Trial Chamber evidently had this in mind, as well, when it reached that conclusion, which now the Prosecution is attempting to interpret differently. According to the Prosecutor, Sljivancanin admitted that he had discussed the outcome of the SAO government meeting, which included references to the transferring of custody of the prisoners of war. What Sljivancanin heard from Mrksic was quoted by the Prosecutor today, and this is his testimony in transcript pages which have been quoted. The content of Sljivancanin's testimony is unequivocal. There is no reference about the information that Mrksic or anyone else ordered the withdrawal of the security from Ovcara. From his testimony, it can be established what we noted in paragraphs 213 and 214 of our response, and that is that Sljivancanin was not concerned because he had received information that the police was there, the commander and the unit. This is what he testified, to the letter, during the examination. When the Prosecutor received this answer, in continuing its probing about the conversation with Mrksic, the Prosecutor did not seek further clarification, nor did they dispute that part of the testimony, and this is on pages 13983 to 13990. Now, if we look at the construction that the Prosecution now is trying to assert, then we can also present our position, in turn, and that is that Sljivancanin had a superior commander. He didn't have any reason to believe that the commander was concealing anything from him. He testified on a number of times and, also, the Trial Chamber established that the commander was fully informed and was making decisions pursuant to that information. Paragraph 389 of the judgement, to which the Prosecutor refers in footnote 199 of their appeal as a reference, which should corroborate that Sljivancanin knew about this decision, does not actually mention at all that Sljivancanin knew about the withdrawal of the security. Your Honours, according to what Sljivancanin said, or in the words that Sljivancanin used, you cannot find the meaning that those words do not contain. That is precisely what the Prosecution is attempting to do right now, to interpret the evidence and the conclusions of the Trial Chamber in their own way. The Defence must underscore here that Sljivancanin was available to the Prosecution for cross-examination for four days and that the Prosecutor could have asked him about any nuance and explanation about their testimony arising from the examination-in-chief, including his conversation with Mrksic. The Prosecutor questioned him in detail about that particular conversation, but there was no mention or no question of hearing what Sljivancanin said in response to this particular question that they are now trying to interpret in their own way. The Trial Chamber could not have based its findings on suppositions. In the situation when one could draw several conclusions or a number of conclusions from Sljivancanin's testimony, any Trial Chamber would need to hold to the standard in dubio pro reo, as it mentioned in paragraph 11 of the judgement. The thesis of the Prosecution about the alleged awareness of Sljivancanin about the withdrawal of the Prosecution is not corroborated by evidence or by the findings of the Trial Chamber. I would just like to also argument [as interpreted] some aspects of the matter covered by Mr. Bourgon this morning. I'm just going to refer to some factual matters that are actually concerned with another question, and also, I would like to address a response that could be prompted by some arguments brought out by the Prosecution. The Prosecution links Sljivancanin's duty to act in -- according to international humanitarian law throughout the afternoon, evening, and night of the 20th of November, 1991, including after the decision on the withdrawal of security. The Prosecution holds the view that he was informed about this decision on withdrawal by Mrksic in paragraph 113 of the appeal brief of the OTP. In our response to question 3, we provided arguments challenging this thesis because the Court did not find that Sljivancanin knew about that decision at any time on the 20th of November, 1991. Therefore, his duty to act in accordance with international humanitarian law after the withdrawal of the security cannot stem from information he might have had on the withdrawal of security. His duty to act in accordance with international humanitarian law can follow from the task assigned to him by Mrksic. That task was linked to the plan of transferring the prisoners of war to the prison in Mitrovica, and after the plan was changed, he no longer had any sort of activity assigned to him in connection with that convoy. It's our case that Sljivancanin was in no way involved in the decision on transferring the prisoners to Ovcara. Even though the Trial Chamber found that there are no elements of any criminal responsibility of his in these activities, at paragraph 660, according to the Defence case, the factual findings in paragraph 659 cannot be upheld, which is why we provided arguments to support our case in our appeal in paragraphs 344 to 365 of our appeal brief. To indicate that the duty entrusted to him by Mrksic was then taken from him, we shall use the arguments of the Prosecutor of two days ago, which we have presented in our closing brief. The Trial Chamber clearly found that all orders, reports, and actions, after the government session, concerning the further direction or location of security and security itself for the prisoners of war, were made bypassing Sljivancanin. Mrksic withdrew the decision on transferring the prisoners to Mitrovica, and I quote the findings of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 607 of the judgement. Then Colonel Mrksic issued a decision that the prisoners be taken to Ovcara, and he carried it out through the staff of the command of Operative Group South in Negoslavci; paragraph 305. Let me remind you that at that time Mr. Sljivancanin was in hospital -- in the hospital. Colonel Mrksic ordered Captain Susic to secure the buses in the barracks; paragraph 298. Lieutenant-Colonel Panic went to Ovcara to convey information to Mrksic about what he had seen there; paragraph 307. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic informed Lieutenant-Colonel Panic on the measures he had taken in Ovcara in paragraph 309. The commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade informed the Chief of Staff of Operations Group South on the spot. These are the findings of the Trial Chamber. Major Vukasinovic briefed Colonel Mrksic on what had happened at Ovcara. That's paragraph 311 of the judgement; and finally, in paragraph 661, the Trial Chamber says that there is no evidence on the involvement of Sljivancanin in the withdrawal of security from Ovcara. Therefore, Mr. Sljivancanin's duty in relation to the prisoners of war ceased when the original task he had been assigned by Colonel Mrksic was changed. And, finally, in answer to the claims put forward by the Prosecutor today, if the Appeals Chamber should find that Sljivancanin was at Ovcara as established by the Trial Chamber, we shall ask what he could have seen there, and in relation to any possible murders, because this is the topic addressed by the OTP, he might have seen his superior officers there making decisions on security; Lieutenant-Colonel Panic and Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. The hangar was in their zone of responsibility. At that time, no one could have foreseen that there would be any murders, and his actions, as the Prosecutor suggests, and his presence in front of the hangar could have had no effect on the later commission of murders. In relation to the arguments put forward by the Prosecution today as to what measures Mr. Sljivancanin might have taken, if the danger that the prisoners of war might be murdered came into being after the withdrawal of the security, as established by the Trial Chamber, and as we have seen, the OTP accepts this in their arguments, then we might ask how the measures suggested by the Prosecutor could have prevented the murders, and how could, as Ms. Brady said, that Sljivancanin might have transferred the prisoners to another location, how could this have prevented the murders if, after that, somebody issued the order that security withdrawn from this other location or, as she suggests, he might have asked that security be reinforced by bringing in more policemen and murders might take place when the security withdrew? What sort of link is there between this bringing in of vast numbers of military policemen or other forces to protect the prisoners if someone later on made the decision that all these guards and the security be withdrawn, or if he took measures to chase away all the Territorials and paramilitaries from around the hangar and then somebody withdraw security? According to the case supported by the Trial Chamber and the OTP, the withdrawal of security ensured the unhindered access to the prisoners by the Territorials and the paramilitaries, which led to the murders. The duty to respond and to prevent any possible murders, if it became certain that there was a danger of murder after the withdrawal, this can be viewed only in relation to the decision to withdraw security. As we have shown, the Trial Chamber did not find that Sljivancanin had any knowledge of that decision. Your Honours, I have concluded our arguments. We will not address any issues related to sentencing, as all this is contained in our written submissions, and we have also made in writing our submissions in response to the Prosecution brief as relates sentencing, and I am at your disposal to answer any questions Your Honours might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Questions, questions? In this case -- sorry, there are no questions, and thank you for your argument and for completing it in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only, as this is my last chance to address you, wish to take this opportunity on behalf of all the Defence teams to thank you for giving us this opportunity to address you and present our arguments, to thank all the participants in the proceedings, and also to express our gratitude to the interpreters because I know what a hard time they had today, trying to keep up with our arguments. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic, for your kind words, and we will now move on to the Prosecutor, Ms. Brady. You have 45 minutes. Following on the salutary example set by the other party, you might prefer not to use all of them, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll definitely heed your words, or we'll try to. Your Honours, I can be quite brief in reply to some of the points that were made this afternoon by Mr. Lukic when responding to the Prosecution's second ground of appeal concerning the aiding and abetting of murder. I will just make a few short points, and then I believe that the majority of this reply will be used by my colleague, Mr. Marwan Dalal, to make some submissions in response to the Article 5 arguments that we heard from Mr. Bourgon. On the question, firstly, of Mr. Sljivancanin's knowledge in the afternoon, on this point we fully realise that this issue is not about merely did he know that the TOs were capable of committing murders. That as much we know as a Trial Chamber finding. But we say, in effect, that it must have been clear that the JNA was unable, largely -- it was -- it can be described as, on the whole, ineffective in stopping the violence. Now, he points to paragraphs -- paragraphs he said we didn't challenge in the trial judgement, such as paragraphs 620, 621. Your Honours, we accept that this is a very nuanced point. We accept, and I said in my submissions this morning, we acknowledge that the JNA was able at times to get some kind of control over the situation pertaining to the TOs and the paramilitaries, and, for example, at some point at the JNA barracks, at some point at Velepromet. But I think, Your Honours, this can be best summarised -- the difficulty of the situation that was clearly pertaining to Ovcara can be best summarised in, actually, paragraph 625 of the Trial Chamber's findings. Those findings, of course, are to be found in the Mrksic section, one could call it, of the judgement, and it -- but it really -- it's a very long paragraph, Your Honours. I don't have time -- or I probably don't have time at the moment to read the whole paragraph to you, but this paragraph very much paints the situation where the situation between the TOs vis-à-vis the JNA was highly volatile. It could have been that there were lulls in violence at times, but the TOs were getting back on top of the situation. The JNA, as I said, was largely ineffective. So when Mr. Lukic says that they were a buffer - they were his words - we ask you to consider, really? Were they really a buffer? And this point that we make, it is not inconsistent with any of our submissions that we made in relation to Mr. Mrksic's appeal, as Mr. Lukic has indicated that somehow we're running an inconsistent case here. We're not. Mrksic did order what we call the last remaining vestiges of protection. Yes, there was some JNA there; of course. This is who he ordered the removal of. But this in itself was insufficient, and then Mrksic orders the last remaining vestiges of this patently insufficient body, the 80th Military Police, the patently insufficient body in the face of this Croat -- this determination by Serb TOs and paramilitaries to harm the Croat prisoners. The second point I'd like to make is regarding the evidence about Velepromet. Mr. Lukic made a submission this afternoon to the effect that the JNA was there and preventing crimes and so that we can't rely on his knowledge that people were killed there to show that the JNA was ineffective. Your Honours, for this, I point you to the evidence regarding whether -- regarding the fact that the Velepromet was, in fact, under guard of the JNA at the time, although the TOs were running Velepromet. Clearly, Velepromet was being used as an assessment centre for finding extremists and possible disguised members of the MUP and ZNG by the Guards Military Brigade OB led by Borisavljevic, and in this regard Sljivancanin himself testified that his subordinate, Borisavljevic, a member of the Guards Motorised Brigade, had been, quote, "given the task of making sure that there was sufficient order and discipline there," and he personally give him that task. That's at paragraph 13603 to 13607. I also point Your Honours to the evidence of Vujic at transcript 4502, who likewise talks of the JNA being at Velepromet when these crimes were happening on the night of the 19th. So I think, Your Honours, the evidence is that the killings occurred that night in Velepromet. The events speak for themselves as to the presence of the JNA at that time. The third point I'd like to mention is the question of his knowledge at 8.00 p.m. We would, of course, argue that it's the only reasonable conclusion, that it's inconceivable that Mrksic omitted and, in fact, actively misled him to believe that the JNA in the form of the 80th was still at Ovcara. He refers to paragraph 661 of the judgement, and Your Honours, if you go to this paragraph, again, it's a paragraph which goes across two pages, it's a very lengthy paragraph, but these essentially -- when you have a chance to look in detail at this paragraph, these findings are essentially the Trial Chamber's findings on whether he was involved in the transmittal of that order to withdraw. And in that conclusion, the Trial Chamber draws the -- makes the findings in Sljivancanin's favour. They do not find beyond reasonable doubt that he was involved in transmitting that order to withdraw through his deputy, Karanfilov. Now, the Trial Chamber goes on to say, as Mr. Lukic pointed out: "He could have been informed by other means, but this is merely conjecture." And this is precisely the point at which we're asking you to make the only reasonable finding which we say is available on the evidence, is that it's not a matter of conjecture. If you take the evidence and you draw the inferences -- the only reasonable inferences that must be drawn from that, Your Honours will be satisfied, we say, about that factual conclusion which the Trial Chamber never really makes because if you look at paragraph 389, that's the other paragraph which connects to this paragraph 661, the Trial Chamber there doesn't make a finding in paragraph 389 about whether he was told about the order to withdraw, so this is where we're asking you to find that the Trial Chamber legally erred as to the expiry of the duty, and then you, yourselves, will be convinced beyond reasonable doubt that he must have learned of the order. I also point out, and it may have been an interpretation error or maybe my colleague misspoke, but he referred to Borisavljevic's having testified about what he told Sljivancanin, and just to point out that Borisavljevic did not testify. The only people who testified on this conversation are Sljivancanin, and we have a small amount of testimony from Vukasinovic. I see my friend nodding, so I think we're in agreement about that point. The final point I want to make is concerning the duty error. Of course, our argument proceeds on the basis that he learned of the withdrawal order. Our argument also proceeds on the basis that he had been entrusted by Mrksic not just in terms of separating and identifying the war crimes suspects at the hospital, but also for their transport and security, and most of the arguments that he makes today on this duty error are really trying to unseat, unpick that factual finding, and this being the Prosecution's appeal, of course, we are entitled to rely on that finding, that he was delegated authority, and not only that finding but the one in paragraph 660, that he, in fact, was also involved in the transmittal of the order to send the prisoners to Ovcara, so those two findings which the Trial Chamber found in our favour, in the Prosecution's favour. That would conclude my submissions, Your Honours, in the reply, and I'd like to now hand over to my colleague, Mr. Dalal, on the Article 5 points. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady, and we'll be hearing Mr. Dalal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will be addressing the Prosecution's reply in the context of our appeal in Ground 1. Before going through my submission, I have three comments to make about the issue of the timing of the attack, which was raised by my learned colleague. The first point is the fact that the military attack ended on 18 November in the finding of the Trial Chamber does not mean that the attack in the meaning of Article 5 also ended, and I don't think there's a dispute between the parties on this question. Indeed, the victimization of the civilian population continued after the 18th of November; for example, in Velepromet, where hundreds of non-Serb civilians were brought from the Vukovar Hospital to Velepromet. Many were severely mistreated, and some were even killed, and this is at paragraph 167 of the trial judgement; see also paragraphs 130, 161, 163, 164, and 177, where also the victimization of civilians is mentioned there beyond the 18th of November. The second point is to say, Your Honours, that after the devastation of Vukovar and its surrounding that the evacuation of civilians was voluntary and based on agreements is not to do justice to the truth. There was a victor in Vukovar and its surroundings that was dominating the geography and the local civilian population, the non-Serb local civilian population. This population was compelled, in fact, to evacuate as a direct result of the relentless bombardment of their homes. They were -- they were still under attack in the meaning of Article 5. And the third and last point on this subject, Your Honours, is that even if we were to accept for the sake of the argument that the attack in the meaning of Article 5 indeed ended on the 18th of November, still the Article 5 requirements, namely, the nexus requirement, is still satisfied based on the law of the Tribunal, and, indeed, crimes -- convictions for crimes against humanity should be entered against the accused as set out in our appeal brief. I now would like to move to the submission -- the prepared submission which addresses your question directly. Your Honours, the attack by the JNA and other Serb forces on Vukovar and its surrounding had horrific consequences. The JNA attacked with aircraft, artillery, tanks, and rockets; paragraph 52. 60 to 75 per cent of the casualties during the conflict were civilians. The Vukovar Hospital, schools, public buildings, offices, wells, the water and electricity supply and roads were severely damaged. Your Honours, kindergartens were shelled; paragraphs 466 and 468. As a direct result of the JNA attack, destruction befell many towns in the Vukovar area, not only in the city of Vukovar; for example, the towns and villages such as Luzac, Opatovac, Stompajvci, Tolonik, Trpinja, Brsadin, Petrovci, Negoslavci, and Borovo Naselje; paragraph 55. Ambassador Herbert Okun, at the time UN special adviser, who visited Vukovar on the 19th of November, observed the city -- observed that the city was completely shattered and compared it to Stalingrad. Ambassador Kypr of the ECMM, on arrival in Vukovar on 20 November, 1991, noted that every house had suffered damage; paragraph 56 and Exhibit 320. Ambassador Kypr of the ECMM described the attacking pattern that had evolved against the non-Serb population in Vukovar and its surroundings. This is at paragraph 43 and Exhibit 312, dated 8th of November, 1991. There were four steps in the description of Ambassador Kypr of this attack. The first one: Tension, confusion and fear is built up by a military presence around a village or a bigger community and provocative behaviour; B, the second step, there is then artillery or mortar shelling for several days, mostly aimed at the Croatian parts of the village. In this stage, churches are often hit and destroyed. The third stage: In nearly all cases, JNA ultimatums are issued to the people of the village demanding the collection and the delivery to the JNA of all weapons. Village delegations are formed, but their consultations with JNA military authorities do not lead, with the exception of Ilok, to peaceful arrangements, with or without --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the speaker could slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: I will slow down. With or without waiting for the results of the ultimatum, a military attack is carried out. And the last stage of the attack: At the same time or shortly after the attack, Serb paramilitaries entered the village. What then follows, and this should be underscored, varied from murder, killing, burning, and looting to discrimination. Your Honours, Exhibit 317 is a video of an aerial view of Vukovar which was tendered through Ambassador Kypr of the ECMM. It shows damage resulting from the widespread and systematic attack against Vukovar and its surrounding. Please show Exhibit 317.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Another exhibit is Exhibit 136, which is a Sky News report that illustrates some of the results of the attack. In it, we can see some of the effects on the civilian population in Vukovar and surrounding, including the damage to the Vukovar Hospital. We will show the first four minutes and forty seconds, approximately, of the report which is, in total, around six minutes and twenty seconds, which speaks for itself. Both exhibits, by the way, were accepted, of course, by the Trial Chamber. Please show Exhibit 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Is there a voice? There should be also a commentary with it. There should be a commentary with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: There should be a commentary with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Maybe in the meantime you could proceed with your argument, and when the system is up, we'll go back to it, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So proceed with your oral argument. It seems to be working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: It appears to be working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It's working, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the time General Zivota Panic was the commander of the 1st Military District and the overall JNA commander of the fighting that took place in Vukovar area. On the 1st of April, 1998, a magazine from Belgrade published an interview with him. In this interview, he was asked the following question: "You are the victor of Vukovar. Could, in the military sense, that affair have been resolved otherwise, without so much destruction?" General Panic's answer was very clear and included the following statement: "If you want to take a city, it is better to demolish it with as few casualties as possible than have people get killed and lose the city." This is at Exhibit 696, pages 5 to 6. Indeed, Your Honours, in conclusion to this part of my submission, the attack against Vukovar and the surrounding was both widespread and systematic. It was not merely a military operation. Civilians were faced with the worst options: death, injury, or displacement. The damage covered all of Vukovar and the town surrounding it. The attacking force wanted to punish the victimised civilian population. For all of these reasons, the attack requirement in Article 5 indeed has been met. I now turn to the issue of the nexus between the acts of the accused and the widespread and systematic attack. Legally, the acts of the accused must be part of the widespread and systematic attack. Two elements need to be established in order to conclude that the acts of the accused were part of the attack. The first one is an objective requirement. The acts need to be sufficiently connected with the attack as opposed to being an isolated act. They need not to be at the midst of this attack. They can be before or after the attack; Kunarac appeal judgement, paragraphs 99 to 100; Tadic appeal judgement, paragraph 251. In Martic appeal judgement at paragraph 318, the Appeals Chamber concluded that the close timing between the attack and the crime, and given that the same perpetrated both -- or were part of the execution of the attack and the crime, the only reasonable inference should be that the crimes were committed as part of the attack. Your Honours are also referred to Krstic trial judgement paragraphs 61 to 67 and the Prosecution appeal brief at paragraph 29 to 30. In this case, the conduct of the accused is objectively part of the attack. First, the Trial Chamber held that at the time relevant to the indictment period, a widespread and systematic attack had occurred in Vukovar and its surrounding; paragraph 472. Second, the context of the conduct of the accused, including its location, is inherently linked to the attack against Vukovar. Indeed, the crimes had been committed in the Vukovar area by the TO and volunteers who played a significant role in the attack itself against Vukovar. And, third, the crimes in question are similar in nature to TO and volunteers' crimes committed during the attack against civilians and prisoners of war alike; see paragraph 47 of the trial judgement, relying on Ambassador Kypr's testimony that on 10 October 1991, Serb volunteers in Lavoc [phoen] had attacked specific homes and killed 22 Croats and 1 Serb; see also paragraph 43 and Exhibit 312, report by Ambassador Kypr, which I have mentioned, and also Exhibit 636, page 2. The second element related to the question of the nexus between the acts of the accused and the attack is the awareness or the mens rea element. The accused must have known that there is an attack on the civilian population and that his acts comprised part of that attack, or at least he took the risk that his acts were part of the attack; Kunarac appeal judgement, paragraph 102. In this case, Sljivancanin and Mrksic knew of the attack, of course, as they were in Vukovar starting from October 1991; paragraphs 465, 664, and transcript pages 13460 to 13461 regarding Sljivancanin. Both Sljivancanin and Mrksic were aware of the violent and lawless conduct of the TO and volunteers which was directed against civilians and POWs during the attack against Vukovar and its surrounding. This conduct included the killing and brutal treatment of civilians and prisoners of war as well as looting and other violent and lawless conduct. And now I would like to refer to some exhibits which demonstrate the knowledge of the accused of the violent conduct of the TO and paramilitaries, the perpetrators of the crime. The first is Exhibit 718. This exhibit Sljivancanin admitted that he had read, and this is in the finding of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 664. It's a report from the 1st Military District, and it reaches also the security organ, which is Sljivancanin's unit. In it, the first page, it says that there are paramilitaries, Arkan's men, that are committing unauthorised killings of arrested ZNG members and arresting Croatian individuals and committing certain acts against them. This is from 18th of October, 1991. The second exhibit is Exhibit 636. It is directed to the 1st Military District, which is the district of the OG South, and it mentions at page 2 explicitly, murderous, violent conduct, albeit not necessarily in the zone of both Mrksic and Sljivancanin, but they should have been aware of this conduct if we also add the other reports to that. It says in a clear wording: "In the combat activity zone of the 1st PGMD, the main motive behind the presence of several groups of different paramilitary formations from Serbia, Chetniks, the Dusan Silni Detachment and various self-styled volunteers, is not to combat the enemy, but to loot the people's property, and" - and this is the most important thing - "engage in the sadistic abuse of innocent civilians of Croatian nationality." Exhibit 415 is distributed order from the commander of both Mrksic and Sljivancanin, Panic, the commander of the 1st Military District, where he mentions the lawless conduct of TO and paramilitary and asks to take action against such conduct. At page 4 of this Exhibit, paragraph 8 : "Every unit must fully control the situation on the territory of its area of responsibility. Commanders at all levels will be responsible for this. Wartime laws have not entered into force, and therefore, as always, nobody has the right to retribution and other kinds of revenge which some local of TO, Territorial Defence, units carried out. In future, arrest those who commit any such acts and undertake appropriate legal measures." And this is from 18th of November, 1991. The last two reports are drafted by Sljivancanin himself. The first one is from 23rd of October, 1991, Exhibit 823, where he talks about the TO and the volunteers' lawless conduct, in this context, looting. He mentions that at the first page -- on the first page: "Searches of personal possessions discovered last quantities of looted items and various valuables which go to show what their primary aims were." And probably most importantly, a report by Sljivancanin, which, also, by the way, these reports get to Mrksic, his superior -- get to Mrksic, a report which is Exhibit 843 from 10 December 1991 by Sljivancanin where he talks about his awareness during the fighting, during the attack in the Article 5 meaning, he writes on page 2: "In addition to the GMTBR, large number of volunteers also participated in the fighting. The volunteers came in groups, individually and with no organisation. Our unit had major difficulties in receiving, checking and equipping them, and in employing them in combat. A large number of volunteers arrived with party insignia, which might have had some considerable effects on the order and discipline of the units conducting combat tasks." These reports, Your Honour, in our submission, demonstrate the awareness of the violent criminal conduct of the TO, which was a constant during the attack in Vukovar, and the accused, both of them, were aware of this conduct. There's a common theme in the criminality of the TO and the attack by the JNA, which is the punishment theme. The perpetrators', and that is in the finding of the Trial Chamber, motivation was indeed to punish the victims, for cultural reasons, probably, but the theme of punishment was clear, and the Appeals Chamber is referred to paragraph 671 for the punishment theme for the attack and paragraphs 47, 532, 535, and 510 for the punishment theme for the crimes themselves that were perpetrated. In conclusion, Your Honours, the Article 5 requirement, namely, the attack, the widespread and systematic attack, as well as the nexus with the acts of the accused, were satisfied, in our submission, and we ask Your Honours to enter convictions for crimes against humanity against both accused as set out in the Prosecution appeal brief in Ground 1. If you have -- unless you have questions, Your Honour, with this, I would conclude my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, we have still one submission with regard to the sentence of Mrksic in reply, unless you have questions, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, you have six, seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dalal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will endeavour to match Your Honours' need for speed, as it were, in the final six minutes and to tread the thin line of brevity and eloquence that Mr. Lukic has already said. Your Honours, in relation to Mr. Mrksic's sentencing submissions, may I just say this: We in our appeal have advanced various grounds, and in particular we focused upon the Trial Chamber's failure to significantly address the position of responsibility that Mrksic held as an aggravating feature in its assessment of the gravity of the crimes. Your Honours will see, when you look at the judgement, that there really is scant reference to this. They touch upon it as being material but say nothing more than that. They do not specifically address it in considering gravity, and in our respectful submission, given the need for a reasoned opinion, they should have done, and this feature of the case in relation to him is clearly one of the most significant features relating to him. Furthermore, they did not specifically address, other than by referring to the fact there had been convictions for them, they did not address the torture and cruel treatment of the prisoners during the course of the afternoon. Clearly, they record that there was a conviction and it happened, but it doesn't appear to have featured in any significant way in their sentence, and certainly, there is no reference to how or in what way they considered it affected the overall sentence that was imposed. And, finally, there's no indication that the Trial Chamber considered the encouragement, the encouraging effect of his inactions on both the torture and cruel treatment and also in relation to the withdrawal on the gravity of the crimes or as an aggravating feature. Again, they -- there's brief reference to it, but really nothing more than that. And if they had properly considered these matters, the sentence would have been significantly higher. And finally, we submit that they started, effectively, from the wrong place. The Trial Chamber said that it could find no comparable cases to assist it, but, Your Honours, we draw your attention to the Vasiljevic Appeals Chamber decision on sentence, which in our submission is the a clear indication of the correct starting point for sentence in relation to aiding and abetting murder and inhumane treatment. In that case - and Judges Guney and Meron may recall it - you imposed a series of 15 years' imprisonment on a low-level perpetrator in relations to five crimes of murder and two crimes of cruel treatment based upon a single incident on the side of the Drina River where the accused person's intent was at the lowest possible level and at which he, the accused, was also at the lowest possible level. Your Honours found, in assessing his culpability, that he had no intent to commit the crimes - clearly, that's why he was convicted for aiding and abetting - but the reason for that was there appeared to have been a very late change of heart or change of mind by the principal perpetrators and that the intent to kill was formed at a very late stage, and so Vasiljevic's involvement as an aider and abetter was simply in escorting the eventual victims from the car to the river and preventing their escape, and their murders, therefore, took place. There was no evidence that he shoot at any of them. That's why he was convicted as an aider and abetter. Now, whilst, of course, we recognise that there are limitations in the comparison of cases as has been recognised here, Your Honours have said in the Celebici appeal judgement that where there are similar factual and legal cases, and we submit these are similar both factually and legally, although of course the rank and responsibility of the accused in each case is different - one at the very bottom and, in our submission, Mrksic at the very top - there clearly are comparisons that could and should properly be made. As Judge Meron recognised in Galic in his dissenting opinion, that a review of comparable cases can assist in determining whether a sentence is "clearly out of proportion" to other comparable cases. In our submission, Vasiljevic is a clear indicator that the sentence for Mile Mrksic is wholly out of proportion. Your Honours, having regard to Mrksic's involvement, whilst we accept that he did not personally carry out the acts himself, as Judge Shahabuddeen observed in Galic in his separate opinion at paragraph 41, after quoting the District Court in Eichmann, that the appellant engaged increased responsibility because, quote, "the degree of responsibility generally increases as we draw further away from the man who uses the fatal instrument with his own hands and reached the higher levels of command." And, Your Honours, we submit that that is as applicable in the case of an aider and abetter as it is in any other case. Mile Mrksic was the commander of Operational Group South. He was well aware of the intent of the killers, although he did not himself share it, but the Trial Chamber found that he anticipated the threat, quote, "would manifest itself in considerable and life-threatening violence and, indeed, death." Trial judgement 621; that the considerable likelihood of serious injury and murder was one that was quote "obvious to Mile Mrksic," trial judgement 621. His mens rea, therefore, whilst not as high, of course, as a principal perpetrator is but, in our submission, a shade away from it and far different from that of the case of Vasiljevic. Of course, in this case the numbers of the murders were far in excess of Vasiljevic, 194, and in addition, 194 victims were tortured, kept in appalling conditions with a palpable atmosphere of fear, and beaten throughout the course of that afternoon and into the evening of the 20th of November, 1991, for which he was also convicted. Your Honours, there is a risk in this case that a sentence of 20 years can seem substantial, but as His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen recognised again in his separate opinion in Galic, the proper question is this: " ... not how the sentence imposed appears in absolute terms. Thus viewed, a sentence of 20 years' imprisonment may appear to be substantial. The question is how the sentence imposed appears in relation to the sentence which is reasonably judged to be merited by the gravity of the appellant's crimes." Your Honours, in this case, the gravity of the appellant's crimes, when compared to the bar set by this Chamber in Vasiljevic, clearly demonstrates that 20 years is inadequate to reflect the totality of his criminal responsibility. A mere five additional years for 189 other murders and cruel treatments and torture, for the encouraging effect of his actions and inactions, for his position of responsibility and his high mens rea in this case, shows that the sentence is manifestly inadequate and one that demonstrably shocks the conscience of the International Community, and we respectfully request that Your Honours revise the sentence, cautious as we appreciate you will be, but this is a case which demands that the sentence is increased, and for those reasons, we invite you, respectfully, so to do. Those are my submissions, unless I can assist you any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it that this completes the case of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: In this case, I think that the tapes -- Registrar, we are all right on the tapes still, aren't we? So in this case I would ask the appellants, Mr. Mrksic and Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I will ask the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, would you like to make a personal statement? THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] I would, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: In that case, go ahead, and I would appreciate if you could remain within the limit of something like ten minutes. THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be brief. I would like to use this opportunity to state once more my regret about the victims of Vukovar, first of all, to the families of the soldiers who were killed, young soldiers, fighters, officers, and the citizens of Vukovar, all those who were killed; also, the fighters defending Vukovar who were killed, and in particular those who were killed at Ovcara. This is something that should not have happened and must not have happened. I can state that I did not order the military police to withdraw. I went to Belgrade, thinking that the assignment would be carried out in the same way that all the previous assignments were carried out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it you have finished. You may sit down. THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you for your statement. Mr. Sljivancanin, would you like to make a brief personal statement? If so, you may do so. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please go ahead. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you, first of all, for making it possible for me to address you at the end of this hearing. I also wish to take this opportunity to express my gratitude to you for giving me provisional release. I abide by all your decisions, and I state that I will continue doing so in the future. Also, I trust that in this case as competent Judges, as in every other case, you will be led exclusively by truth and justice because the law cannot be just if it is opposed to truth and righteousness. I addressed the Trial Chamber at the beginning of my trial and also at the very end of the trial, thus taking the opportunity to state what I expected from the trial. I abide by everything I said on those occasions. I believe you are aware of what I said, and I do not wish to repeat myself. In addition to this, I testified for more than a week about everything I have been charged with in the indictment. My testifying was a condition I immediately put to my Defence counsel, and I state again before the Court and the public everything I know about the charges against me. The second condition I put to my counsel was that only those witnesses be called in my Defence who wished to come of their own free will to testify here, and that not a single one of them must ask for any protective measures. Had someone like that turned up, I would have desisted from calling that witness because I did not wish any witnesses to appear before the Court who are afraid of anything, and there were, in fact, no such witnesses. Only public and sincere testimony can remove the stain from the honour of the members of the JNA who were killed in Vukovar carrying out their soldierly duties, and only the full truth and not prejudices can bring peace to the families of the victims in their misfortune. I wish to state once more that I regret all the victims in this war. I have heard many very moving testimonies in the courtroom. The families of the victims have the right to know what happened, and by my testimony and through my Defence, I wish to contribute to this. Unfortunately, in spite of all this, even after the trial, it turns out that much of the truth has been concealed. I spent most of my life in the army. That army played a large role in shaping my values and virtues. It taught me to be courageous. Those who are courageous are not afraid of the public. They're not afraid of the truth. Therefore, I hope today that you, as honest men and women, because that is what Judges are, will not allow injustice to prevail over justice in this case. Your Honours, I am used to doing everything I do in public. I did everything I did in Vukovar publicly. Some experience me as a Communist wearing a five-pointed star, of which I was proud. Others saw me as an aggressor. But I wished and tried to do professionally the job I had been trained for, and I had taken an oath I would perform. Some saw this as a sin, but I am proud of it. If it's a sin that I believed in a country in, which nobody else seems to have believed at that time, and that I performed the job I was bound by law to perform, then my belief was my mistake, but I do not lose my faith. I have not lost it, and I believe that you, Your Honours, will reach the decision that I am not guilty. Finally, when it has now turned out that I'm the last to address you, I wish to repeat the words I said at the beginning of the trial, and I hope that everyone in this courtroom will accept these words. They were written by our Nobel Prize-winning writer, Ivo Andric. I quote: "There is not much justice in the world, but the less justice there is, of more value it is. It is slow, yes, and it is often late, but sooner or later it arrives. That's why I say, rely on justice and be not afraid." Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sljivancanin, for your personal statement. You may be seated. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: This brings us to the end of this hearing and of this appeal case, and I would like before rising to thank the parties for their participation, the appellants, the lawyers for both the appellants and the Prosecution, and, of course, the staff, the Registry, and especially the interpreters, who had a very, very difficult task and performed it extremely well, and I really would like to congratulate them for the level of the interpretation, which was so essential to an effective hearing of this case. I suggest that we reconvene at quarter to 4.00 for the status conference. I understand that the Registry needs about 30 minutes to change the tapes. We will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: to be followed by a Status Conference. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
